cards.name: Sheoldred, the Apocalypse
cards.prose: I have… thoughts about this. Benedict Cumberbatch aside, Sheoldred, the Apocalypse is an unbelievably powerful card. While it provides no card advantage whatsoever and might simply die to removal, the simple fact that it punishes your opponent for trying to find that removal is the most crippling part about it. All the while, nothing can get into combat with it, and you get to buffer your own life total. Sheoldred is a menace and likely one of the best cards in this set.

cards.name: Excalbian Gamemaster
cards.prose: Okay, this is just absurd. Excalbian Gamemaster is the quintessential “army-in-a-can” creature, giving you a minimum of two 1/1s when it enters and probably a lot more than that if you’ve built around it. It’s even very splashable so that no matter what, if you’re a deck built around strange new worlds, you’ll be able to play this. I wouldn’t be surprised if this was the best card in Star Trek Limited.

cards.name: U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit
cards.prose: The U.S.S. Enterprise-A, Free Spirit has to be one of the strongest spacecraft we’ve ever seen. It’s essentially a Baneslayer Angel that also creates three 1/1s on entering. It only requires six charge counters to become a creature, which the three 1/1s can provide over the course of two turns. Even if your opponent can deal with this spacecraft, you still got your free tokens, so it’s not even that bad for you. This is how you design iconic aspects of the show! The Enterprise is one of the most recognizable spacecraft in all of pop culture, and this being one of the strongest cards in TRK is

cards.name: U.S.S. Discovery, at Black Alert
cards.prose: When designing the card, U.S.S. Discovery, the Black Alert , of course the discover mechanic made sense to use. Getting to discover 5 when Discovery enters or attacks is huge, and it’s even one of the easier spacecraft to station! I don’t think anyone’s beating this card too frequently, it’s just such a beating to get buried in card advantage this way.

cards.name: Captain Jean-Luc Picard
cards.prose: Here, we have the best Captain in the whole show (fight me), Captain Jean-Luc Picard . Legendary actor Patrick Stewart brought this incredible character to life through 10 TV seasons (across TNG and Picard) and four movies, and he is one of my reasons for loving this show in the first place. Picard’s greatest strength as a captain was in the way he inspired and mentored his crew, so of course the card gives +1/+1 to your whole team and creates more officers whenever you cast creatures or spacecraft. I don’t think you’re very likely to search for any spacecraft with its final ability, but I lov

cards.name: Overflow Submatrix
cards.prose: I don’t think I had a new riff on Lurrus of the Dream-Den on my bingo card for Star Trek , but it does look like that’s what we have in Overflow Submatrix . They may come with finality counters , but the ability to recast any artifact creature in your graveyard over the next few turns is incredible. I’d always try to wait for an opening where I can cast this with, say, 5 mana available, allowing me to get a free 2-drop on the same turn I play it, then hope it survives long enough to get more free creatures. This card is incredible, and a great early sign to draft a Borg deck.

cards.name: Holo-Engineer
cards.prose: Before we even get to the rest of the card, Holo-Engineer starts out life as a 3/3 that creates another 3/3 for just 4 mana. That’s already incredible, and you should play it in every green deck. Now, what can we do with its other ability? There are a lot of different tokens in this set, such as the 1/1 Officer s, 2/1 Klingon s, and Treasure s, any of which you can choose to upgrade into 3/3s if you have this card in play. This has the potential to be an absolute must-kill, and there are so many combos with it that it’ll just take a little bit of creativity to break wide open.

cards.name: Decree of Pain
cards.prose: For all its different reprints, we’ve not actually seen Decree of Pain in a 1v1 Draft set since it was first printed in Scourge back in 2003. I’m not often in the habit of casting 8-mana spells, but a board wipe that draws a bunch of cards sounds very appealing. This is something I’d want to take early and then make sure I had the mana acceleration to hit it often. It’s also fantastic if you cycle it, so you can’t really go wrong.

cards.name: Bristly Bill, Spine Sower
cards.prose: I just want to say that representing McCoy as Bristly Bill, Spine Sower is a stroke of genius. Also, Bristly Bill is a spectacular card. Putting a +1/+1 counter on something with every land you play is incredible, and in the late game, its activated ability is often better than using your mana to cast a new spell. It’s a must-kill threat, and if you play this early enough, it takes over the game. Excellent card!

cards.name: Q, Stacking the Deck
cards.prose: John De Lancie’s mysterious “Q” was a recurring villain from The Next Generation who also showed up in Deep Space Nine and Voyager , a seemingly omnipotent being who would act as a constant annoyance to Picard and the rest of the Enterprise crew. And this weird card design really does suit him. Sometimes, you’ll play Q, Stacking the Deck , exile a pretty weak spell and not much will happen. But, if you exile anything good with it, then every single card you draw, lands included, can become copies of that card. If you hit a bomb rare, a removal spell, or anything else on that level, you basical

cards.name: Borg Cube
cards.prose: One of the things that made the Borg so distinctive was the intimidating design of their ships. They were simply massive cubes or spheres floating through space, and seemingly impossible to penetrate. Borg Cube looks obscenely powerful. If you’ve built a strong black/white deck, the affinity should bring its cost down to around 3 or 4 mana, so you can use it as a removal spell. Stationing it may prove difficult, but your reward if you do so is the ability to assimilate the creature you removed in the first place. I’m hesitant to give this a flat 10/10 due to its high costs, but this looks like

cards.name: U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class
cards.prose: The legendary ship captained by Jean-Luc Picard, the U.S.S. Enterprise-D, Galaxy-Class is one of the more powerful spacecraft in this set. It essentially gives you an impulse draw the first time you station it in a turn, which is something you can easily control. If you play it right, you can get a ton of free card advantage from this one card. Better yet, you can keep stationing it even after it becomes a creature and keep the card advantage flowing. The Enterprise-D is a phenomenal card and probably one of the strongest first picks in the entire set, given that any deck can play it.

cards.name: Georgiou, Terran Emperor
cards.prose: Georgiou, Terran Emperor is a fun and unique design for a 6-drop. As much as I’d love to go down to 0 life and start creating hordes of officer tokens, the fact that you’ll lose as soon as it leaves play makes this strategy a bit delicate. Though if your opponent can’t remove it at all, you’ll inevitably win. Georgiou is going to be a temperamental card for sure, but one I’m definitely willing to try out.

cards.name: The Caretaker
cards.prose: Facing dilemmas seems remarkably easy to do in Star Trek , and The Caretaker has got to be the best payoff for them. You can trigger it in every end step , so instant-speed modal spells might be able to add up to two triggers every turn cycle. The Caretaker may be a 6-drop, but a few free spells plus a 5/6 vigilance creature makes a huge impact in any game you’d play it in.

cards.name: Death Is Irrelevant
cards.prose: Weirdly enough, Death Is Irrelevant looks basically unplayable in Borg decks. Casting an 8-mana spell in a low-curve aggressive deck simply isn’t going to happen. That said, if you have a deck that can resolve an 8-mana spell, then this will almost always win you the game. Reanimating an indestructible creature from either graveyard every single turn, including the one where you play this, gets out of hand extremely quickly. What’s especially nice about this is how likely we are to have big creatures in graveyards thanks to the landcyclers, so there should always be something for you to bring

cards.name: Mr. Spock, Science Officer
cards.prose: Perhaps the most recognizable character in all of Star Trek , Leonard Nimoy’s Mr. Spock, Science Officer is a unique card that can double every single card you draw . Normally, these effects don’t let you draw an additional card in the draw step, but Spock does. It may not prompt you to draw a card like Quantum Riddler might, but your opponent can’t possibly allow Spock to live for too long since you’ll be drawing two cards every turn. I’m inclined to say Spock is very good. It just needs to survive long enough to give you the value you’re due.

cards.name: Elim Garak, Simple Tailor
cards.prose: There are so many dilemmas you can face in this set that I’m definitely keeping my eye on any and all dilemma payoffs. Elim Garak, Simple Tailor looks like a very strong one to me. It may not give you card advantage, but a 4-point total life swing can be obscenely powerful, and it doesn’t even come with a once per turn clause. Given that we’ve seen many dilemmas that cost very little mana, I could see Garak trigger several times in a turn and really put a lot of pressure on your opponent.

cards.name: Dr. Leonard "Bones" McCoy
cards.prose: The final member of our original bridge crew in this review, Dr. Leonard “Bones” McCoy was a brilliant doctor with a good dash of southern charm. His metaphors, hostile personality, and close personal relationship with Captain Kirk turned him into a much-loved character across the whole show. This card is also excellent, basically functioning as a sort of Eternal Witness with flash who can also save a creature from dying if you flash it in at the right time. I’d always play Bones in a green deck, because it’s hard not to get any value from it.

cards.name: The Inner Light
cards.prose: Another of The Next Generation ’s greatest episodes, The Inner Light sees the Enterprise encounter a probe in deep space that forces Picard to live out a lifetime as a member of a long dead alien race. It’s a beautiful story, and it makes for a very powerful saga. Reanimating a creature and then potentially drawing a bunch of cards is well worth the mana cost here, and it doesn’t take much to support it.

cards.name: Nog, Ambitious Cadet
cards.prose: On its own, Nog, Ambitious Cadet can attack as a 3/4 with menace on turn 3 and immediately surveil. From there, if you level it up to its final ability, Nog can easily give you a bunch of free land drops, which also give you the added benefit of having cards leave your graveyard. This is a neat little package that looks unassuming at first but could add up to a significant advantage in a very short span of time.

cards.name: Crystalline Entity
cards.prose: The Crystalline Entity was an early “villain” in The Next Generation , an all-powerful entity that the Enterprise crew couldn’t figure out how to stop. It was highly destructive, so seeing it here as a massive creature that wipes the board when it enters seems very appropriate. It’s worth accelerating into, and you can play it in any deck willing to do that, which makes it sound like an incredible bomb.

cards.name: Rishkar, Peema Renegade
cards.prose: All the value you get from Rishkar, Peema Renegade is given to you upfront. You don’t need to wait around; you just immediately get your two +1/+1 counters, one probably going on Keenser and the other on your 2-drop. That’s simply excellent, and it gives you quite a sizable early lead in any game in which you play it.

cards.name: Tatyova, Benthic Druid
cards.prose: Tatyova, Benthic Druid is one of my favorite “mythic uncommons” of the past. The fact that it draws you a card every time you play a land means you naturally draw into more lands and can keep triggering it every turn. Tatyova was a big disappointment when it returned in Foundations , but this set’s architecture is built around lands so much more.

cards.name: Ertai Resurrected
cards.prose: Even though each ability lets your opponent draw a card, it’s hard to feel too scared of anything your opponent might do if you sit back with an Ertai Resurrected in your hand. Countering or destroying anything at instant speed and putting a 3/2 onto the board is phenomenal. It’s as simple as that.

cards.name: Stella Lee, Wild Card
cards.prose: We’ve never had Stella Lee, Wild Card in a Draft set before, but it looks really good. Blue/red’s archetype is based around noncreature spells already, and there are a lot of cheap cantrips that help to enable this. Beam me up is especially good for helping you cast two spells in a turn, so I have no trouble believing this will be a bomb in the right deck. Try to grab a couple copies of Make It So to aim for an infinite combo.

cards.name: Antagonist Incorporator
cards.prose: Antagonist Incorporator looks like a great way to swarm the board with additional Borg tokens. Your Borg decks already want to go wide, and not only does this help you to do that, but it also rewards you for it. Plus, the tokens you make also have this ability and can create even more tokens. The only thing that could hold this back is that you need to connect with your creatures to get them to trigger, and that might not always be possible, but this feels like an incredibly powerful card if you can enable it.

cards.name: General Chang, Cold Warrior
cards.prose: What usually holds sacrifice decks back is their lack of good, cheap sacrifice outlets. General Chang, Cold Warrior is very cheap both to cast and to activate, but it also gives you an extremely powerful effect, putting counters on all of your Klingons at once. This is a great payoff for that deck, as well as being a useful 1-drop to start off your curve as early as possible.

cards.name: Deanna Troi, Psychic Counsel
cards.prose: Deanna Troi, Psychic Counsel in TNG is one of the things that made the show look so ahead of its time, and the card is quite good. Troi’s very good when you cast it early and a lot of your creatures enter with counters, and less good the later you play it. On balance, that makes this card pretty good in most creature-heavy white decks.

cards.name: Seven of Nine, Unassimilated
cards.prose: Seven of Nine is without a doubt one of the most interesting characters in the whole franchise. Rescued from the Borg by the crew of Voyager , she embarks on a journey to reclaim her humanity and individuality. Seven of Nine, Unassimilated portrays her at the end of her story, as Captain of the new Enterprise-G . This card can’t do much in combat until you have enough lands, but giving you a free loot every turn is good enough in the meantime. I don’t think getting to seven different lands is that unreasonable, and five should be pretty easy in the right deck, which makes Seven quite a reasona

cards.name: Armus, Skin of Evil
cards.prose: In one of TNG’s most unexpected episodes, the crew discover a planet inhabited by only a single lifeform: Armus, Skin of Evil . They try to engage with it and… let’s just say it goes very wrong for them. This card is really powerful, too. I honestly prefer it as just a good 3-mana removal spell, but coming down on 7-mana and pressuring the opponent’s hand can also be devastating in the right matchup.

cards.name: Salt Vampire
cards.prose: We really have come a long way since the days of Mesmeric Fiend . We don’t see new versions of this effect very often, but when we do, it’s often an upgrade on the previous one. Salt Vampire is an excellent play on turn 2. Even if it’s going to die at some point, taking a card out of your opponent’s hand for a while will mess up the plays they were planning to make. You should probably always take a cheap removal spell that could kill this, but no matter what you take, this should be pretty effective.

cards.name: Captain James T. Kirk
cards.prose: Few characters in science fiction are quite as prolific as William Shatner’s Captain James T. Kirk . As Captain of the Enterprise , he never shied away from getting his hands dirty, and hand-to-hand brawls were common in the original series. As the character didn’t believe in no-win scenarios, it stands to reason that this card’s ability would get stronger when you have no options left in your hand. While none of Kirk’s modes are all that strong, having it trigger on entering and attacking means they’ll add up very quickly. This is an incredible design for an iconic character, and one of the c

cards.name: Captain Jonathan Archer
cards.prose: I never watched Star Trek: Enterprise , but if I had known that Captain Jonathan Archer had a lovely dog , I might have given it a try sooner. Three mana for a 3/3 plus a 1/1 is a great start, but you also have three creature types between Archer and Porthos, meaning its activated ability will already give +3/+3 at minimum. This will probably let Porthos attack as a 4/4 or bigger, or be able to send some other creatures into combat instead. This is a great card for any green deck just on rate alone.

cards.name: Captain Pike, Fullness of Time
cards.prose: Most people know who James T. Kirk is, but far fewer will know that in Star Trek ’s pilot episode in 1966, Christopher Pike was in fact the captain of the Enterprise . He was then replaced by William Shatner in the second episode, but since those days, Pike’s character has been explored in the Kelvin timeline films and two of most recent projects: Discovery and Strange New Worlds . Captain Pike, Fullness of Time of course had to use this mechanic and does so quite well. I don’t know how big it’s likely to get, but even if Pike were just a 2/2 that let you play lands off the top of your deck ,

cards.name: Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy
cards.prose: One of Deep Space Nine ’s main characters, Jadzia Dax, Living Legacy is doing a pretty fair impression of a Badgermole Cub . While nowhere near as broken, Jadzia still sits back and creates large amounts of extra green mana for you. You can even use other cards to put +1/+1 counters on it and speed up the process. If you cast Dax on turn 2, it lets you play a 4-drop the following turn and then a 6-drop the turn after. Most mana dorks don’t do that. Plus, if you draw Dax late and it’s now bad to play, use it as a combat trick instead! A pretty solid card all round.

cards.name: Gowron, Eager for Battle
cards.prose: As you’d expect from a rare, multicolored Klingon in this set, Gowron, Eager for Battle is the perfect sacrifice outlet for the deck. By sacrificing a Klingon to Gowron, it gets a +1/+1 counter, trample, and you draw a card. That’s a great deal, and we’ve already seen several Klingons that wouldn’t mind dying a glorious death in battle to galvanize their leader.

cards.name: The Destruction of Praxis
cards.prose: Board wipes are very powerful in Limited, but the biggest downside they have is that your opponent gets the initiative to make the first play after the dust settles. If you have six different lands in play, sweeping away all creatures and then creating a pair of 2/1s with haste is an absurd effect. I’m still unsure as to how easy it’ll be to get up to six different lands, but assuming it’s regularly possible, The Destruction of Praxis has a chance at being among the best cards in Star Trek .

cards.name: Miles O'Brien, Transporter Ops
cards.prose: Before Colm Meaney’s Miles O’Brien became the chief of operations on Deep Space Nine, he was the Transporter Chief aboard the Enterprise-D in The Next Generation . Whenever a story involved some sort of transporter malfunction, Chief O’Brien was there to pick up the pieces. As such, it’s very fitting that Miles O'Brien, Transporter Ops beams up a creature when it enters and then rewards you at the end of any turn in which you returned anything else to your hand). None of the archetypes in Star Trek are specifically centered around this mechanic, but Chief O’Brien is still a very good payoff fo

cards.name: Lieutenant Commander Data
cards.prose: Perhaps the most beloved character in Star Trek: The Next Generation , Lieutenant Commander Data was a highly sophisticated android whose character arc centered around his quest to better understand humanity. This mythic card does quite a lot if you can enable it. Removing three +1/+1 counters from your creatures to draw cards doesn’t sound all that appealing. However, removing charge counters from fully stationed spacecraft that can easily pick them back up again? That sounds a lot more interesting. Data also grows itself with every noncreature spell cast by either player, which makes it a ve

cards.name: U.S.S. Reliant, From Hell's Heart
cards.prose: The Reliant is the ship in Wrath of Khan that Khan commandeers and takes into battle against Kirk and the Enterprise . U.S.S. Reliant, From Hell's Heart looks like it has a lot of potential. Reanimating one creature right away makes it worth spending the mana to play it, even though 10 charge counters is a lot to accrue if you want to attack with it. Once you do reach 10 counters, reanimating a creature whenever this hits an opponent is a huge bonus, and not one that your opponent can ever let you get to.

cards.name: Transporter Malfunction
cards.prose: I always try to pay attention whenever I see a removal spell that I can cast twice. There are so few removal spells with flashback in the game, let alone ones that are this efficient. You’d happily play Transporter Malfunction even if it didn’t have beam me up, so the fact that it does is a huge boon. This is bound to be one of the best removal spells in Star Trek , and it can even finish off a player.

cards.name: Locutus, the One Who Speaks
cards.prose: In one of The Next Generation ’s best plot twists, the season three finale sees the Borg assimilate Picard into their collective, giving him new life as “Locutus”. Locutus, the One Who Speaks is an incredibly powerful Borg payoff, giving +1/+1 to all your artifact creatures, including itself. If that doesn’t take your fancy, Locutus is also a removal spell that you can use from your hand. This card is awesome and one of the reasons I’m excited to build a Borg deck in Limited.

cards.name: Kenrith, the Returned King
cards.prose: No matter which colors you have in your deck, Kenrith, the Returned King should be powerful. Its abilities are expensive, but beyond the red one, any one of them can win you the game if you activate it over and over.

cards.name: Empress Galina
cards.prose: When Empress Galina was first printed, there were very few legendary permanents in the game. You might have 10 or so in a set to help tell the story. But in a Universes Beyond set, that number is very different. There are 104 legendary permanent cards in Star Trek , and Galina can steal each and every one of them. Yes, you have to untap with it and it adds almost nothing to the board by itself, but once you steal even one creature, you stand to win the game off Empress Sato’s back.

cards.name: Torbran, Thane of Red Fell
cards.prose: The triple red on Torbran, Thane of Red Fell is definitely a downside, but the effect you get is incredibly powerful. I especially like how this will buff the damage from both the 1/1 Officer tokens and the 2/1 Klingon tokens. Just be aware that you may want to skew your mana base a little to help accommodate for its cost.

cards.name: Riku of Many Paths
cards.prose: When it was announced in the late 2000s that there would be a new Star Trek movie with a brand-new recasting of the original Enterprise crew, fans were understandably excited. Leonard Nimoy was then announced to be appearing in a cameo role, but his Spock ended up being a main character and integral to the plot of the film, which perhaps explains why William Shatner wasn’t invited…. Anyway, Riku of Many Paths only worked with plot cards in Outlaws of Thunder Junction , but in a set with as many modal spells as this one, it looks incredibly powerful!

cards.name: Scotty, Miracle Worker
cards.prose: His Scottish accent may have been questionable at best, but James Doohan’s Scotty, Miracle Worker became an integral part of sci-fi history as the Enterprise ’s chief engineer. As soon as I heard about the beam me up mechanic, I immediately assumed Scotty’s card would use it, maybe even give it to all the cards in your graveyard. And hey, that’s exactly what Scotty does! You still need to have access to some creatures to bounce to pay for the costs, but getting to recast even one or two good spells will make playing Scotty well worth those costs.

cards.name: Captain Kathryn Janeway
cards.prose: Captain Kathryn Janeway looks quite strong. Exploring is a fairly random mechanic; you’re not sure what you’re going to get out of it, but allowing every creature you play to explore should help you to smooth out your draws and make sure you’re finding the best spells you can.

cards.name: Captain Benjamin Sisko
cards.prose: The badass captain of Deep Space Nine , Captain Benjamin Sisko functions kind of like a Hero of Precinct One but for dilemmas. I’ll happily take that. There are so many modal spells and abilities in Star Trek that this seems like a great card to take early and build around. I don’t think we’re likely to use Sisko’s 5-color activated ability , but it’s still very good without it.

cards.name: Sela, Tal Shiar Paradox
cards.prose: One of the most memorable plot twists in TNG was the reveal of this Romulan character, played by Denise Crosby, whose own main character on the show, Tasha Yar, had been killed off a few seasons prior. Sela, Tal Shiar Paradox is first and foremost an excellent payoff for the black/green graveyard deck. While it’s a self-contained advantage engine, getting to attack with Sela doesn’t seem too promising when it’s only a 3/3 for 4 mana. Even without attacking, sitting back and generating free tokens whenever something leaves your graveyard is an excellent way to spend your mana, so long as you su

cards.name: Sulu, Space Swashbuckler
cards.prose: Oh my, indeed! The legendary George Takei brought Mr. Sulu to life, the pilot of the Starship Enterprise . Sulu, Space Swashbuckler recreates one of the character’s most iconic moments from the show with a heck of a lot of style ( editor’s note: Yes, we know that “Oh, my!” is a George Takei meme, not something Sulu ever said ). A 2/2 for 2 with first strike is already very annoying to deal with, but then any equipment or spacecraft you play will let Sulu draw you a free card, especially if you have a spacecraft to station. I expect Sulu to be a very solid build-around card, but you don’t even

cards.name: Wesley Crusher, Starfleet Cadet
cards.prose: “Shut up Wesley!” – Captain Picard Perhaps one of the most divisive characters in Star Trek , Wesley Crusher was a young upstart boy genius who aspired to become a full Starfleet officer. I personally loved the character, but there we go. Wesley Crusher, Starfleet Cadet has a lot of possible options going for it. While each of these options are relatively weak and situational, the fact that you get two of them gives all sorts of possibilities. On top of that, it’s a great candidate to beam up, removes tokens , creates dilemmas, and more. Wesley is a great card even with such narrow abilities.

cards.name: Collation Trimatrix
cards.prose: The main reason Cryptbreaker was so good back in the day was for this ability right here. Collation Trimatrix may not be able to create any tokens , but getting to draw a card just by tapping three of your Borg is an incredible ability. If you’re lucky enough to curve this on turn 1 into Assembly Specialist on 2, I doubt you’ll lose that game. This is an awesome payoff for the Borg, something I’d be happy to take early and build around.

cards.name: Academy Instructor
cards.prose: Like most playable Young Pyromancer variants, Academy Instructor is still cheap enough to be worth playing. On top of that, it also triggers with every noncreature spell you cast, not just instants and sorceries. This is the perfect build-around for the red/blue archetype, and it also puts a lot of extra power onto the board for red/white.

cards.name: Nyota Uhura, Communications
cards.prose: Lieutenant Uhura, played by the wonderful Nichelle Nichols, made waves as one of the first black television characters in a major role in any genre, let alone science fiction. When you play Nyota Uhura, Communications , you should probably name 2 or 3, as they’re the most common mana values of cards in Limited decks. As we get more used to the format, I’m sure a more accurate choice will present itself. If you play Uhura on turn 3, on the play, then choosing 3 will usually net you at least one card, and hopefully more as the game progresses. While it won’t always pan out as you want, I think U

cards.name: Hive Mind Coprocessor
cards.prose: If you have successfully “gone wide” by the time you play this card, you should theoretically be able to get an attack in and probably draw several cards for doing so. The fact that you don’t need to pay mana into the triggers from Hive Mind Coprocessor makes it a lot easier to use, too. I can definitely see this being the top-end you need for a good Borg deck, especially as the extra cards should help you to keep applying pressure in future turns.

cards.name: Khan, Vengeful Heart
cards.prose: Khan Noonien Singh is perhaps Star Trek ’s most legendary villain. The mythic representing him is quite strong in Limited, but casting Khan from exile isn’t likely to happen too often. Not a lot of things in Star Trek will exile it, but just casting Khan, Vengeful Heart once to sacrifice something and draw two cards is good enough.

cards.name: Tasha Yar, Out of Time
cards.prose: Tasha Yar, Out of Time is a fast, aggressive creature with a great death trigger, and you can bring it back later for one final hit. Tasha gives you quite a lot of advantage for a single card; you just have to find ways to make the most of it.

cards.name: Constable Odo
cards.prose: The ability I like the most on Constable Odo is naturally the double investigate. Two Clue s is the easiest way to turn Odo into card advantage, but having a nice tempo play by stunning a creature for a few turns is certainly going to come up from time to time, too.

cards.name: Kirk, Commanding Officer
cards.prose: We’ve not seen a lot of good reasons to care about getting to 8 power’s worth of creatures, despite it being the red/white mechanic. Kirk, Commanding Officer is a good reason though. Impulse drawing a card when you attack, no matter whether Kirk itself attacks, is really powerful and also something you can repeat turn after turn. This red/white deck doesn’t look very promising, but Kirk at least is something worth building around.

cards.name: L'Rell, Fierce Visionary
cards.prose: Sacrifice decks are always going to want access to as much sacrifice fodder as you can give them. L'Rell, Fierce Visionary is perfect for providing you with an endless stream of Klingon tokens to sacrifice, which should then pair well with the sacrifice payoffs we’ve seen.

cards.name: Seven of Nine
cards.prose: You can’t ask for much more than drawing a card whenever you face a dilemma. We know from past experiences that this is among the best kinds of payoff for a Draft archetype, and dilemmas are extremely well supported in Star Trek. Seven of Nine is an excellent build-around for blue/black.

cards.name: Spock, Always Your Friend
cards.prose: We’ve seen a lot of creatures similar to this in the past, like Augur of Bolas or Wandering Mind . They’re typically very good, and Spock, Always Your Friend isn’t only a good rate for this, but also lets you pick up artifacts and enchantments, giving you a much wider range of available options. Spock is an excellent enabler for this blue/red deck and also one of the best creatures we’ve seen to pair with beam me up spells.

cards.name: Vash, Freelance Archaeologist
cards.prose: I think the archetype that impresses me the most in terms of payoffs is the black/green one. We’ve seen several good ways to have things leave your graveyard for profit, and Vash, Freelance Archaeologist is just another great reward for that. There’s not much else to say. This archetype looks cool, and Vash is excellent in it.

cards.name: Encounter the Unknown
cards.prose: Two damage to all creatures is the base rate on this card, and I think that should be pretty good. We’ve seen a lot of small creatures in the format so far, which leads me to believe it’ll be quite effective. Also, the fact that you can trade Encounter the Unknown for two cards from your deck if you don’t need it is a really nice buyout when you come against creatures too big for you to destroy.

cards.name: Pah-Wraith
cards.prose: Most decks you build will have at least two differently named lands. Namely, the two basic lands for your two colors. As such, Pah-Wraith will basically always attack as a 6/4 with first strike at minimum. On top of that, giving +2/+0 to your team looks pretty good. The problem is that this is a 7-drop that’s best suited for a low-curve aggro deck, which doesn’t want 7-drops. It looks good, but I have a feeling it’s just too expensive to be the massive bomb that I think it could be.

cards.name: The Wrath of Khan
cards.prose: I’ve mentioned it a few times already, but 1982’s Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan is believed by many Trekkies to be the best Star Trek project ever produced. This card does a reasonable job of telling this story, and it’s quite powerful, too. It’s basically a 3-mana removal spell that deals 4 damage and then has some minor upsides on top, which is something you’d always play.

cards.name: Replicator
cards.prose: I’ve been playing Pauper a bit recently and am learning how powerful Campfire can be, simply because it’s a cheap artifact that sits in play and gains you life every turn. Replicator has a lot of that same energy going on, as you can just copy the Food token it gives you every turn and use them to stay alive. On top of that, this set has quite a few Clue tokens and 1/1s lying around for you to copy, so I’d imagine it shouldn’t be too difficult to use Replicator every turn for something good.

cards.name: 70,000 Light-Years from Home
cards.prose: The plot of Star Trek: Voyager involves the fledgling crew of the U.S.S. Voyager as they end up on the other side of the galaxy, 70,000 Light-Years from Home . So yeah, exiling a creature or spacecraft is a pretty resonant ability for this card to have. It’s basically a much weaker Path to Exile , but Path is so powerful already that that’s hardly a bad thing. You probably won’t want to play this early, but exiling a big creature in the late game so efficiently should be great.

cards.name: Subcommander T'Pol
cards.prose: Subcommander T'Pol is quite a powerful creature. I’d already be very happy to have a Frost Lynx with flash , effectively giving you an additional turn of that creature being stunned. The real bonus here is the ability to counter an activated or triggered ability, which Tishana's Tidebinder has shown us can be quite devastating in the right scenarios. The choice of one or the other is incredible too, and it even presents a dilemma, making T’Pol a high pick in Draft.

cards.name: Resistance Is Futile
cards.prose: We don’t see a lot of clean 2-mana removal spells anymore. While Star Trek does have a considerable number of artifact creatures, including all of the spacecraft, Resistance Is Futile still answers a lot of creatures that need to be dealt with. Unlike Go for the Throat , it has a very reasonable extra mode that you can use instead. This is an incredible removal spell, and it’s ticking a lot of boxes for this format.

cards.name: David and Carol Marcus, Creators
cards.prose: We’ve seen plenty of similar 3-drops that accelerate you with an extra land and they’ve always been great, but David and Carol Marcus, Creators even fixes you for every color by giving you a New Planet token. The card’s just great, and you should play it in every green deck you can.

cards.name: Hologram Stalker
cards.prose: If you were looking for a good payoff for the black/green archetype, look no further than Hologram Stalker . Six mana gets you a good card out of your graveyard, a 2/2, and a 3/3. Incredible! Then, anything else you get out of the graveyard later creates another 3/3. I call this a payoff for black/green, but it’s honestly so strong on rate that every green deck should play it, and it’s likely the best green uncommon in Star Trek .

cards.name: Daniels, Temporal Agent
cards.prose: You had me at Gravedigger . Daniels, Temporal Agent is a powerful two-for-one play that should be in any deck that can feasibly cast it, plain and simple. In black/green specifically, its second ability gives Daniels a built-in way to leave the graveyard and trigger all of your payoffs for a second time. This card is awesome and so clean. Pick it early, and often.

cards.name: Malfunctioning Holodeck
cards.prose: I love the flavor behind this card. In TNG, the Holodeck would frequently malfunction, trapping its users inside it until the problem could be resolved, so of course this is a Banishing Light variant. Malfunctioning Holodeck is your standard white removal for the set, but being an artifact should also help it to play well with TRK’s themes.

cards.name: Rutherford, Upgraded Ensign
cards.prose: Getting to look at your top six cards means that if you’ve built your deck correctly, Rutherford, Upgraded Ensign will hit an artifact very often. Let’s say there are 10 artifacts left in your deck when you play Rutherford on turn 3. That gives you a 92.63% chance to find at least one artifact. I’ll take that deal any day.

cards.name: Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist
cards.prose: You don’t need any other creatures on the battlefield for Hoshi Sato, Exolinguist to be worth playing. It counts its own creature types, so you should always be able to look at two cards and pick the best one. If you do have other creatures, you get to look at potentially a lot more cards and cherry pick something very good. At the bare minimum, it’s a cantrip creature, assuming your opponent doesn’t remove this scientist before its trigger resolves, at best it’ll find you the best card in your deck while adding to the board.

cards.name: D'Ghor Bloodletter
cards.prose: Given how common the 2/1 Klingon tokens and the 1/1 Officer tokens are, the ability to give -1/-1 to all creatures sounds like it could be quite devastating. D'Ghor Bloodletter , despite being a Klingon, is actually a great weapon for fighting against the Klingon decks, and the Fleshbag Marauder mode is a nice buyout for the right situation, too.

cards.name: Eject the Warp Core
cards.prose: Vayne's Treachery was among the best commons in Final Fantasy Limited with good reason. The ability to kill any big creature for just 2 mana, even at the cost of another sacrifice, is very powerful. Eject the Warp Core is exactly the same card, and I have no trouble assuming it’ll be just as good in this setting.

cards.name: In the Pale Moonlight
cards.prose: One of Deep Space Nine ’s best episodes, In the Pale Moonlight sees Captain Sisko reflecting on the personal cost he’s paid in attempting to trick the Romulan empire into joining the Federation’s war against the Dominion. This saga tells that story pretty well and is a very strong card to play. It reminds me of The Eldest Reborn , where every chapter of the saga gives you another bit of value, and I’m all here for that.

cards.name: Khaaaaaaaaaaaannn!
cards.prose: This heavily memed moment from Wrath of Khan obviously had to be made into a card of its own, but I don’t have to like it. The card is a fine piece of removal. Khaaaaaaaaaaaannn! will deal 2 damage for 2 mana, 4 damage for 3, 6 damage for 4, and so on. These are all good rates, and the combination of all of them in the same card is really good.

cards.name: Syndicate Liquidators
cards.prose: Giving two +1/+1 counters to any target creature is a really nasty effect to have on this creature. While Syndicate Liquidators is an obvious home for them since it has trample, it’ll often be better to spread the love and put the counters elsewhere, since this will already be a prime target for your opponent’s removal spells. What scares me most is that we’ve seen several ways to get multiple land drops in a turn, so I could definitely see a turn when Syndicate Liquidators grows from a 4/4 to a 10/10 and just goes to town.

cards.name: Engineered Explosives
cards.prose: Engineered Explosives is a classic Magic card that has been a competitive mainstay for over 20 years. If you have access to more than just two colors, it allows you to destroy just about anything your opponent might put in front of you, which is incredibly flexible for an otherwise colorless removal spell . It’s a bit expensive to use, but that flexibility can’t be beaten.

cards.name: Mikaeus, the Lunarch
cards.prose: Mikaeus, the Lunarch was an absolute bomb when it was first printed 15 years ago. Nowadays, power creep has settled in a little bit. This feels a fair bit worse than Reality Fracture ’s Guiding Hydra , though it’s still strong enough that you should always play it in a white deck.

cards.name: Thada Adel, Acquisitor
cards.prose: Blue decks in TRK Limited are bound to have a few artifacts in them, so Thada Adel, Acquisitor is likely to be an unblockable 2/2 that rips apart your opponent’s deck, potentially giving you a bunch of free cards too. Against nonblue decks, you’ll have to find a way to make it unblockable, but about a quarter of the cards in Star Trek are artifacts, so you’re bound to find some good stuff to steal.

cards.name: Prosper, Tome-Bound
cards.prose: Prosper, Tome-Bound is one of the most popular commanders in my local scene, and for pretty good reason. Having it sit there and effectively draw you an extra card every turn is very powerful. But not only that, your opponent simply can’t attack a lot of creatures into a 1/4 with deathtouch.

cards.name: Minamo, School at Water's Edge
cards.prose: Starfleet Academy is situated on the San Francisco Bay, right next to the Golden Gate Bridge. How fitting for it to be here as Minamo, School at Water's Edge . This land is obviously very good, especially with the number of legendary creatures in this set. It’s a strict upgrade over an Island , and it’ll be a differently named land for the Strange New Worlds deck. You can’t afford to take it too highly in Draft, but it should always make your deck when you do.

cards.name: Phyrexian Tower
cards.prose: Lands that can tap for 2 mana should never be underestimated. Phyrexian Tower shouldn’t be randomly put into any deck, but if you have enough sacrifice fodder for it, it should be extremely powerful.

cards.name: Shizo, Death's Storehouse
cards.prose: Much like Minamo, Shizo, Death's Storehouse is a strict upgrade over a Swamp and an additional land name to enable the strange new worlds mechanic, so you should always play it. Fear is a strong evasive ability too, so you should definitely be able to use this to break some board stalls every now and again.

cards.name: Primary Unimatrix Adjunct
cards.prose: Double strike is an extremely powerful ability, so giving it to your whole team should be pretty good. My main problem with Primary Unimatrix Adjunct is just how vulnerable it looks. It does seem like you’d need to protect it if you want any chance of it surviving, and having it die in the middle of combat puts your other creatures at risk.

cards.name: He's Dead, Jim
cards.prose: Well, every set worth its salt has one of these. Four mana to destroy any creature at instant speed and give a minor bonus on top is always good, usually one of the best commons in the set, and nothing else needs to be said about it. I do love the theming of using one of McCoy’s best-known lines, He's Dead, Jim , as the card’s name.

cards.name: The Duras Sisters
cards.prose: A 3/2 with a very good death trigger for just 2 mana is really good. Better yet, having a hybrid mana cost means that you’ll never fail to cast The Duras Sisters on turn 2 in a black/red Klingons deck. This is just the perfect aggressive 2-drop for that deck, and something I’d prioritize early.

cards.name: Phlox, Unorthodox Doctor
cards.prose: I do love to draw some cards as a reward for doing what an archetype wants, but Phlox, Unorthodox Doctor isn’t quite that simple. Having your creature deal combat damage to a player as well as have a counter on it means there are two ways in which this could go wrong. Phlox is certainly powerful, but you do need to put in a bit of extra work to make it pop off. Keep in mind that this automatically works with spacecraft, since they’ll have charge counters on them when they’re attacking.

cards.name: D-7 Battle Cruiser
cards.prose: Creating a temporary 2/1 token with haste every turn isn’t a bad effect in theory, but is it worth the cost for this card? I’m not entirely sure. These tokens can be pretty useful in the early game, and they give you a free sacrifice every turn, but once they’re outclassed in combat, they’re very difficult to get any advantage from. This D-7 Battle Cruiser looks to be on the weak side for a rare spacecraft, but I could be wrong.

cards.name: Mirror Universe Intrusion
cards.prose: Creating a permanent clone of a creature is one thing, but to have that restricted to only creatures your opponent controls is worrying. Mirror Universe Intrusion has the potential to be a back-breaking card, but if your opponent controls no creatures or only weak ones, it does next to nothing. I might be too harsh with this one, but I don’t like it when cards have big downsides like this.

cards.name: V'Ger, the Intruder
cards.prose: This is one hell of a big payoff for a ramp deck . V'Ger, the Intruder does everything I want out of a 7-drop. As a 5/7 flier, it should close out games relatively quickly. It immediately draws a card when it enters and then again whenever it attacks, but if you’re worried about getting attacked, it can shrink opposing creatures instead. You can’t just put a 7-drop into your deck, but any deck with a bit of mana acceleration will be happy to pick this up.

cards.name: The City on the Edge of Forever
cards.prose: Widely regarded as the best episode of the original series, and I’m inclined to agree, The City on the Edge of Forever sees a deranged McCoy time travel back to the 1930s and inadvertently alter the present so that Starfleet never existed. As Kirk and Spock chase after him, they meet Edith Keeler, and from there a moral dilemma unfolds that you really have to see for yourself. It really is incredible. Anyway, the card tells this story excellently, and it provides enough value that it looks like it should be worth playing.

cards.name: Picard, Leading by Example
cards.prose: While effects like this one are best when you can use them at instant speed, the fact that Picard, Leading by Example starts out by giving +2/+2 means that it can turn just about any creature into a legitimate threat. Make this creature any bigger and now your 1/1s can attack as 4/4s or even 5/5s, pushing through enemy blockers. This ability also puts more power on the board for the red/white archetype, which might be a big help. Picard is a very aggressively-slanted creature, but white’s decks mostly look like they want to attack a lot, so it should be able to find a home in any of them.

cards.name: U.S.S. Excelsior, Cutting Edge
cards.prose: Destroying a tapped creature isn’t always going to be something you can do, but when you can, the U.S.S. Excelsior, Cutting Edge will be a strong two-for-one. While it will be hard to station, as long as you get to remove a creature, you don’t even need to do so right away. There are also a few ways to pick it back up and reuse the triggered ability , which makes it a very useful card if you can utilize it correctly.

cards.name: Tell Me What You See
cards.prose: In this classic TNG episode, Picard is captured by the Romulans and is subjected to psychological torture through gaslighting. His captor keeps insisting that he’s being shown five lights when there are only four, but our intrepid Captain never compromises, always repeating that there are just four lights. While Tell Me What You See uses a punisher mechanic that we don’t often like, the fact that it’s repeatable as long as you keep facing dilemmas makes it look very appealing. I think this is going to be a really cool build-around for this deck and I’m excited to see where it lands.

cards.name: Khan, Despot by Design
cards.prose: I’m very high on Khan, Despot by Design given the context of set. We’ve seen a lot of creatures with only 1 toughness, including the 1/1 Officer and 2/1 Klingon tokens. That should mean that Khan has a lot of opportunities to come down and devastate a board. On top of that, it’s also a big trample creature that’s kind of hard to deal with in its own right.

cards.name: Sarcophagus, Ship of the Dead
cards.prose: A lot of the value of Sarcophagus, Ship of the Dead is given to you up front, as even before it’s stationed, it’s basically an Orcish Oriflamme . Of course that’s not enough to justify the whole grade; that +1/+0 boost not only helps you in combat, but also helps you to station. Ten charge counters is a lot, but between its own trigger and power boosts, that number starts to look a lot smaller, and a 4/4 flier looks incredible in this format.

cards.name: Will Riker, First in the Field
cards.prose: As a frequent member of landing parties, Will Riker, First in the Field is all about landfall. While having no landfall triggers itself, Riker creates two landfall triggers every turn. I naturally worry about running out of lands at some point, but that might be to your benefit, as it means you just draw spells for the rest of the game. I wouldn’t want to run Riker without a good foundation of landfall triggers to make use of it, but it looks really good if you can give it that support.

cards.name: Amok Time
cards.prose: Known to Trekkies as simply “the one where Spock gets horny”, Amok Time is a classic episode where Spock experiences “Pon Farr”. This requires him to return to Vulcan and meet his arranged mate, but it results in him and Kirk having a fight to the death. This card is a fantastic retelling of that story, and if you play it right, it’ll end up being a removal spell that gets a creature back from your graveyard and even gains you 3 life for good measure. This is an excellent card, and you should take it highly.

cards.name: Species 8472
cards.prose: The trouble with playing any 6-drop is the massive loss of tempo you’ll feel if your opponent is able to remove it as soon as it hits the board. But if your 6-drop gains a bunch of life when it enters, that helps to offset that tempo loss. Species 8472 does exactly that, and it might even gain as much as 5 or 6 life in a good Strange New Worlds deck. This is exactly the sort of big thing I’d want to ramp into in that deck.

cards.name: Cleveland Booker, Empath
cards.prose: Even if they can’t block, creating a free 2/2 token on landfall is an incredibly powerful ability. Especially considering the fact that there are many ways to give yourself additional land drops each turn. Cleveland Booker, Empath looks perfectly suited to any aggressive landfall deck, but the “can’t block” clause on these tokens likely prices it out of being included in other decks for value.

cards.name: Planetary Bombardment
cards.prose: One mana for 4 damage is truly an absurd rate, which is why Flame Slash still sees play in Vintage Cubes to this day. Planetary Bombardment is mostly just a sorcery speed Shock , but the fact that it does have this potential to kill bigger creatures so cheaply is likely to make it one of the best red commons, if not the best overall.

cards.name: Sylvia Tilly, Joy of Discovery
cards.prose: Tilly was, by far, my favorite character in Discovery . She was so sweet and pure, and her struggles with anxiety and self-doubt were inspiring to me at a difficult time in my life. Her card, Sylvia Tilly, Joy of Discovery , has a few things going on. It’s primarily a payoff for the graveyard deck. Tilly can theoretically give you a +1/+1 counter each turn, but I feel like you won’t be able to fill your graveyard often enough to fuel that for too long. Instead, it gives a nice bit of value when it enters, and then triggers your black/green cards when you need it to. Can’t ask for much more tha

cards.name: All Good Things...
cards.prose: Perhaps not the episode I’d have chosen here. All Good Things. . . was The Next Generation ’s final episode. It sees Picard, tasked by Q, attempting to solve the mystery of a spatial anomaly from three distinct points in time simultaneously. This naturally gives way to a saga that does the same thing three times and culminates in a final ability. Just like the name suggests, this saga gives you “all good things”. Five mana to draw six cards and exile three is a pretty good deal. The 10 life is definitely not irrelevant either, and it gives you a big incentive for exiling three lands if you can

cards.name: MACO Strike Team
cards.prose: I’m sure that MACO Strike Team is going to be incredibly annoying in Constructed, but it seems a bit underpowered for Limited. The fact that it triggers from any of your creatures being targeted is fantastic, but as a 2/1 creature itself, it’s extremely weak and vulnerable. It’ll trade off in combat for no value and often won’t even be able to attack.

cards.name: Hemmer, Fixing What Is Broken
cards.prose: I was frankly hoping for more out of the signpost uncommon for spacecraft. Perhaps even a powerful spacecraft? Hexproof is a cool ability to give, but Hemmer, Fixing What Is Broken isn’t an exciting enough payoff to move in on this color pair. This is clearly worth playing, but I doubt I’d even miss it if my white/blue deck failed to find one.

cards.name: Cloak and Phaser
cards.prose: Cloak and Phaser looks like an incredible payoff spell for strange new worlds. At 6 mana it’s very castable, but a little too expensive. At 5 or less it’s incredible. To accomplish this, you only need three or more different lands, which sounds very doable. In a good build of strange new worlds, the thought of getting to cast this for significantly less mana doesn’t seem all that unlikely either. This card is a very real incentive for this deck, and one I’m going to be very excited to build around for myself.

cards.name: Assembly Specialist
cards.prose: Two mana for a pair of 1/1s is always a good deal when we get it. When you add in the fact that the Borg want to be a go-wide aggro deck centered around artifact creatures , Assembly Specialist looks like one of the best ways to start your curve in that deck. I’d prioritize this very early when drafting a Borg deck. It’s less good but still solid in other white decks.

cards.name: Ghost of Illyria
cards.prose: There are a lot of good enters triggers in Star Trek , so it shouldn’t be too hard for Ghost of Illyria to shine in. Most of the spacecraft also have triggers you can utilize, since this works with any nonland permanent. Sorcery-speed flicker effects aren’t usually that strong, but like any spell, attaching it to a creature with good stats changes that equation enormously.

cards.name: Dominion Saboteur
cards.prose: Five mana is a little on the expensive side for a Clone , but that really shouldn’t matter. These types of creatures are always fantastic, and Dominion Saboteur is no different. Not only can it copy any creature or artifact on the battlefield, but it also copies the counters on it, so you can also copy a fully stationed spacecraft. No matter what, this will always be the strongest creature on the battlefield once you play it, and it’ll be well worth taking early in a draft.

cards.name: Jett Reno, Problem Solver
cards.prose: Easily one of the best characters in Star Trek: Discovery , Jett Reno, Problem Solver is quite a nifty little build-around for the dilemmas deck. It’s hard to know how frequently you can trigger it, but I’d imagine that a good version of this deck can do so with relative ease. I doubt you’ll be able to get it to 4 power very often, not for a lack of ways to trigger it, but because it’ll take so long that an opponent will probably remove Reno before it happens. Still, there are other ways to buff its power and get to draw cards; you just need to find some ways to enable it.

cards.name: Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior
cards.prose: I’m sure Worf would be the one to tell you that a warrior is patient and waits for the right moment to strike. Worf, Honor-Bound Warrior is perfect for sitting back, building up counters, and then striking when it’s big enough to attack profitably into your opponent’s blockers. This Worf doesn’t even need to attack to look threatening, and your opponent will likely need to deal with it at some point, which is a big compliment for a 2-drop 1/1.

cards.name: Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign
cards.prose: Brad Boimler, Eager Ensign is one of the main characters from one of the animated series, Lower Decks . While I’m not very familiar with the show, this card is extremely good. A 2/2 lifelinker for 2 mana is a great start, but Boimler pulls a bit of double duty by being a great build-around for both white/blue spacecraft and white/green counters. You can use it to quickly station a spacecraft or just get extra utility from your various doctor creatures, and both sound pretty good.

cards.name: Federation Field Medic
cards.prose: You had me at “draw a card”. I sincerely hope to always be able to draw a card off of Federation Field Medic . But if we can’t, it’s still pretty good to play it as a 3/2 plus a +1/+1 counter, so this is just a great card for the +1/+1 counters deck.

cards.name: Guidance Failure
cards.prose: So yeah, we’re back to this design again. Four mana for an instant that puts a target creature on the top or bottom of its owner’s deck. We’ve seen so many variations on Guidance Failure that we know it’s going to be good, especially with the cost reduction to help slot it into more places on the curve.

cards.name: Gabriel Lorca, Mirror Menace
cards.prose: The surprising villain of Star Trek: Discovery ’s first season, played by the brilliant Jason Isaacs, Gabriel Lorca, Mirror Menace is a pretty annoying card. A 5/4 with menace for 5 mana isn’t all that great, but the ability to keep bringing Lorca back whenever you face a dilemma certainly paints it in a new light. It’s both a dilemma payoff, and a card that keeps leaving your graveyard. I think you need to find the right deck for it, but Lorca will be pretty powerful if you find it.

cards.name: Organic Avulsion Unit
cards.prose: Menace on one creature isn’t a problem. Your opponent can usually deal with it without too much fuss. But menace on your whole team? That’s dangerous. Consider a board where both players have three creatures. If you give all your creatures menace and attack, your opponent can only block one of them, leaving them to get hit by the other two! For this simple reason, Organic Avulsion Unit actually looks pretty scary, despite its weak stats.

cards.name: Munitions Enthusiast
cards.prose: You don’t need any additional abilities to make a 3/2 trample for 2 mana worth playing. Munitions Enthusiast is a great early play in any red deck, and it trades up extremely well, since the 1 extra point of damage will help it kill bigger creatures in combat.

cards.name: Adversary by Algorithm
cards.prose: Adversary by Algorithm gives us effectively a reprint of Call of the Herd , except with beam me up. I really like that, and with how good Bestial Incursion was in Reality Fracture , I have no problem thinking this will be very good here, too.

cards.name: Common Goal
cards.prose: We do prefer these spells to be instants, but letting two of your creatures team up to destroy another means that Common Goal ought be a very effective removal spell in any green deck. It’ll basically always find something to kill.

cards.name: Temporal Conqueror
cards.prose: We’ve seen this exact card in previous sets between Temporal Conqueror , Eccentric Farmer , and Ostrich-Horse , which all varied in power level. In Star Trek , getting the land back from your graveyard triggers gravebreak effects, allowing it to be an even better card later in the game. Temporal Conqueror is definitely going to appear on my shortlist for best green common in the set.

cards.name: Zero, Incorporeal Sensate
cards.prose: As far as annoying little artifact creatures go, Zero, Incorporeal Sensate is certainly up there. It’s essentially an uncommon Elite Spellbinder that also works with all of your Borg payoffs, despite not being a Borg itself. This kind of disruption won’t do a lot, but it might force an opponent to switch plans or not commit a powerful card to the board when they wanted to, which is more than enough to warrant playing this card.

cards.name: Sickbay
cards.prose: Five mana is a lot for this effect, maybe too much. Sickbay at least gives you a +1/+1 counter on the turn you play it and then gives you two counters on any turn in which you played a creature. Food tokens turn into three additional counters, and playing the planet duals also rewards you with extra counters. There’s a lot to like about where all of this is going, but I just wonder if 5 mana is too much to enable it all.

cards.name: The Unicomplex
cards.prose: Each of these lands provides you with what should be a strict upgrade over a basic land of the same color, with a very minor bonus when they enter. They each surveil 1, which we know from past experiences is a very good thing to do for free, and the additional modes that they have are also quite interesting, especially on The Unicomplex . You should generally take these a little higher in your pick order than a random dual land, but still not over premium spells for your deck.

cards.name: Jhoira, Weatherlight Captain
cards.prose: In case you’re unaware, a “historic” spell is any artifact, saga, or legendary spell. Jhoira, Weatherlight Captain is pretty good, allowing you to draw a lot of free cards if you have a deck that can support it, but being a Hill Giant in stats definitely holds it back a lot.

cards.name: Mogis, God of Slaughter
cards.prose: If you can enable the devotion on Mogis, God of Slaughter , then it’s obviously very good. My main concern is that Star Trek is very much not set up to enable that. Most red and black permanents in the set have only single color pips, and if Mogis is not a creature, it’s just too slow to make any kind of meaningful impact. Double-pipped hybrid cards might be able to help here.

cards.name: Talon Gates of Madara
cards.prose: It’s pretty cool to be able to hide a protection spell in your land base like this. Talon Gates of Madara looks pretty strong to me. We’re already happy playing it as Unknown Shores with upside, and sometimes it’ll be really powerful when you get to use its ability at the right time.

cards.name: Romulan Bird-of-Prey
cards.prose: Two mana for a 4/4 with flying is obviously an excellent deal, but you have to go through a few extra steps to get there with Romulan Bird-of-Prey . You could station it if you wish, but you can also get there just by casting noncreature spells as you normally would. I only wish that your reward for doing so was better than a vanilla flier. I’m sure this card will be fine, but it’s not something I’d look to take highly.

cards.name: Plasma Cascade
cards.prose: Plasma Cascade isn’t exactly Lightning Strike , but it’s still a good deal for 3 mana. I love the extra bonus that’s been tacked onto it too, as trading an excess land for a better card is very close to just drawing a card.

cards.name: Worf, Intelligence Contractor
cards.prose: Worf was the first Klingon officer to serve in Starfleet, and he’s the most used character in the entire franchise. This card, Worf, Intelligence Contractor leaves quite a bit to be desired. It naturally works very well in a Klingon deck, where you should be able to sacrifice the creature that you steal, but being limited to only stealing smaller creatures will likely hold Worf back.

cards.name: Dr. Joseph M'Benga
cards.prose: Dr. Joseph M'Benga is interesting, but the main thing to note about this doctor is that it doesn’t do anything by itself. Doubling all your counters is a good ability to have access to, but unless you’re using counters quite frequently, M’Benga basically does nothing.

cards.name: Dal R'El, Augment Orphan
cards.prose: Having seen just how aggressive the landfall deck appears to be, this card disappoints me. With all of its extra lands, this deck shouldn’t have much trouble with mana, and Dal R'El, Augment Orphan does virtually nothing to advance the aggressive game plan. This card isn’t bad, but it’s not a gold card I’d look to pick up early.

cards.name: The Doctor, EMH
cards.prose: At the bare minimum, The Doctor, EMH represents a 3/3 and two +1/+1 counters for 5 mana, which is exactly what I’d expect for that mana cost. If you have any other +1/+1 counters in play though, you can get so much more out of it. The Doctor can always put its counter on itself to maximize the number of counters you can get, and if it ends up putting four or more counters on board, that mana cost starts to look like a bargain.

cards.name: D'Vana Tendi, Optimistic Ensign
cards.prose: While 3-drop mana dorks aren’t the greatest, D'Vana Tendi, Optimistic Ensign gives you something good to spend your extra mana on. I’d happily play this in any blue/green deck, but I’d fear that the double color pips in its cost might hinder its playability in a deck that’s only one of its colors.

cards.name: Watery Grave
cards.prose: They may be some of the strongest dual lands in Magic, but in Limited the shock lands aren’t much different from any other dual land. They’ll be great for fixing your colors and for enabling strange new worlds, but that’s about as far as it goes.

cards.name: Gul Dukat, Colonial Prefect
cards.prose: The villainous Cardassian, Gul Dukat, Colonial Prefect , probably won’t do as much damage in Magic as the character did in Star Trek . While the card’s ability is certainly interesting, the fact it costs 7 mana is a significant drawback. While 7-drops are definitely castable in modern Limited formats, they need to make a much bigger impact to the board than this, especially as Gul Dukat might not even do anything on the turn you play it. I think my grade is quite generous here. It might just be unplayable with the way the format shapes up.

cards.name: Rok-Tahk, Budding Scientist
cards.prose: I really don’t get this card. Even at 4 or 5 mana, I don’t think it’d be good, so at 6 mana I’m baffled. Rok-Tahk, Budding Scientist is simply over-costed and doesn’t do something that a 6-drop wants to do. The indestructible Murf token is kind of interesting, but it’s such a weird reward for casting a 6-mana beater.

cards.name: Hit It!
cards.prose: Giving all your creatures haste definitely isn’t worth playing a whole card for, so the power of Hit It! has to rely on its other ability. I really dislike how it’s only very likely to ramp you and not simply guaranteed. I just know that small percentage chance will come back to bite me often enough to hate this card. I’ll play it and it’ll probably work, but I won’t be all that happy about it.

cards.name: Conquest Mission
cards.prose: While taking a turn off to play Conquest Mission doesn’t sound too appealing, giving you a free 1/1 every single time you play an artifact sounds absolutely incredible. This clearly rewards you for building your deck to maximize it by filling it with as many artifacts as you can find. Knowing that the Borg power each other up just means that a black/white deck with this card will be able to get even more value out of it. This is a build-around that I’m very excited to play with, and I hope it works.

cards.name: H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship
cards.prose: In Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home , Kirk and the Enterprise crew travel back in time to rescue a pod of Humpback Whales and bring them to the 23rd century. The H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship is the captured Klingon warbird that they use to do this, making this an incredible top-down design. There are two whale cards in Star Trek , one of which is the blue landcycler, so it should be relatively easy to find one or two to pair with this card. You get the upside right away by getting to tutor for one, and you might even be able to attack with it on the following turn as well as get the extra tur

cards.name: Bat'leth
cards.prose: Three mana to give -2/-2 is pretty inefficient by most standards, but the classic Klingon Bat'leth gives you quite a bit more than that, leaving behind a very relevant piece of equipment in addition to the removal. We’ve seen this play out twice now in the last couple of sets; Lich's Relic was one of the best cards in Reality Fracture and Crude Bent Blade was among the best commons in The Hobbit . I’m sure this Klingon weapon will be very similar.

cards.name: Grand Nagus Zek
cards.prose: The Ferengi, introduced in Star Trek: The Next Generation , are basically extremist capitalists, where their entire culture and society is built around the acquisition of wealth no matter the cost. So, of course Grand Nagus Zek and the other Ferengi we see here will be Treasure -themed. Creating a free Treasure whenever something dies is pretty good on its own, especially in a Klingon deck where we expect our creatures to die more often. I don’t know what I make of Zek then getting bigger, because the Treasures are probably best used as further sacrifice fodder or mana acceleration. Either way

cards.name: Exploratory Mission
cards.prose: This is a very interesting card advantage engine. It essentially reads as Landfall: Draw a spell”, which honestly sounds really powerful. Like the other cards in this cycle, Exploratory Misson is a 4-mana enchantment that doesn’t affect the board, so its power level is naturally limited.

cards.name: Sarek, Federation Ambassador
cards.prose: Sarek was a recurring character in multiple Star Trek projects as both Vulcan’s ambassador to Earth and Spock’s father. Sarek, Federation Ambassador simply asks you to control five or more creature types to draw a card. Given that most creatures in this set have two creature types and there’s very little overlap, this effectively means you need three creatures in play, including Sarek. That sounds very strong, and it also scales extremely well if you can theoretically get up to 10 types.

cards.name: Deep Space 9
cards.prose: Well then. The titular space station of its own show, Deep Space 9 looks like one hell of a big win condition. Potentially four entirely free permanents every single turn is absolutely incredible, and it even spots you the first four as soon as it enters. And that’s not to say anything about stationing it and giving a massive +3/+3 to all your creatures. DS9 is almost guaranteed to win you the game if you get to play it, the only problem is finding a way to cast a 9-drop, but I’m definitely up for the challenge.

cards.name: Hologram Janeway
cards.prose: I often talk about the effect of Luminarch Aspirant and how broken it is in Limited. Hologram Janeway has a remarkably similar effect, but with a lot of extra hoops to jump through. Those hoops don’t seem too prohibitive, so I could see this being a very good card in the red/white deck where it belongs, but also with black/white Borg and artifact creatures.

cards.name: Shields Up!
cards.prose: Just like Take Up the Shield before it, Shields Up! should be a highly effective combat trick that protects a creature against just about anything. While costing 2 mana isn’t ideal, hexproof and indestructible covers pretty much all your bases and makes it worth playing.

cards.name: Energize
cards.prose: This card reminds me a lot of Silent Departure , a very powerful interactive spell in its own right. Like its predecessor, Energize , gives you two potentially powerful tempo spells. They may be sorceries , but resetting a spacecraft, removing an annoying blocker, or whatever else is well worth playing this card for.

cards.name: Interstellar Effigy
cards.prose: Usually, we like our Man-o'-War s to be much cheaper than 5 mana, but Interstellar Effigy can still get the job done. It may come down later in the curve, but bouncing a creature while adding to your board is still very powerful. Also, it’s a common, when most cards like this tend to be uncommon, so we’ll see it far more often.

cards.name: Suurok-Class Science Vessel
cards.prose: It’s 3 mana and it draws a card. I’m sold. While I doubt this will be as good as cantrip creatures of the past, Suurok-Class Science Vessel still has all the hallmarks of a brilliant common for blue. It even has one of the smallest station requirements at just five charge counters, meaning the various engineer cards should have it up and running in no time at all.

cards.name: Zefram Cochrane, Warp Pioneer
cards.prose: Played by the brilliant James Cromwell in Star Trek: First Contact , Zefram Cochrane, Warp Pioneer was the inventor of warp drive who made first contact with the Vulcans, ushering in an era of peace for the whole world. Getting to play artifacts from the top of your library is quite a powerful ability, but it’s still possible that you just won’t see anything when you play this pilot . It’s definitely worth playing Cochrane in an artifact-centric deck, but I’m a little apprehensive that it does little else if you don’t get to cast any spells with it.

cards.name: Blastoneuron
cards.prose: This theme of having cards leave your graveyard for value appears to be well-supported. Blastoneuron ’s enters trigger isn’t the most useful thing you can do, but having a flying creature sit around and trigger over and over sounds pretty good to me. It’s surely not going to trigger as often as something like Falkenrath Noble , but if you can support it properly, it might be closer to that than you’d think.

cards.name: Boarding Action
cards.prose: Getting to play Boarding Action on turn 2 and immediately attack is a great way to start a curve. Later in the game, you might even find a good spot to cast this twice with its beam me up cost and get a great attack in with your two new haste creatures . This looks like an excellent red common that most of red’s archetypes will be very happy to play.

cards.name: La'An Noonien-Singh, Security
cards.prose: Since La'An Noonien-Singh, Security only requires you to attack to trigger, you can often trigger it on the same turn you play it. With at least 4 power already on the board, La’an can come down and allow you to attack profitably past a single blocker. From there, the ability to take a blocker out of the equation each turn should allow you to attack far more often, making this a pretty strong card for an aggressive red deck.

cards.name: Tal Shiar Analyst
cards.prose: Thermo-Alchemist was one of my favorite spells build-arounds from the past. Tal Shiar Analyst , despite costing an additional mana, is practically the same card. That mana definitely matters, but what you get for it is a creature that’s also capable of attacking for more damage and maybe even trading for something in combat if you need it to. For a common, this looks like an immensely powerful card in blue/red.

cards.name: Jake Sisko, War Correspondent
cards.prose: Eumidian Terrabotanist is already a fine card, so throw in the ability to investigate sometimes and you have a very nice card. There are a couple ways to enable that second land drop naturally, and you’ll be very happy if Jake Sisko, War Correspondent is able to turn the odd ramp spell into extra Clue tokens.

cards.name: Saru, Unthreatened
cards.prose: As the moral compass of the U.S.S. Discovery , whenever Michael Burnham strays, Saru is there to set her back on course. Therefore, it’s very appropriate to see Saru, Unthreatened as a creature who saves another creature from danger. Being a 3/2 itself is also a really nice rate for its mana cost, so I’d play Saru in basically any green deck.

cards.name: U.S.S. Voyager, Lone Wanderer
cards.prose: The classic U.S.S. Voyager, Lone Wanderer of course has to do with lands. The Voyager crew became the first in Starfleet to explore the uncharted Delta Quadrant on their way home to Earth. We normally see some variants on Explosive Vegetation in sets these days, so seeing it attached to a spacecraft makes me think this one will be very strong. This is of course best suited for Landfall or Strange New Worlds decks, but it’s strong enough to see play elsewhere if you need it to.

cards.name: Xenobotanist
cards.prose: Yep, a 2-drop mana dork in green . Xenobotanist is a great card. It fixes your mana, and you should take it very highly.

cards.name: Andromedan Automatons
cards.prose: This is going to be a really fun challenge during a booster draft. The first copy of Andromedan Automatons is basically unplayable, but once you find a second one, the first one you play draws you a spell when it enters. That’s pretty good, and if you find a third or even a fourth copy, they get even better.

cards.name: Free Borg Revolutionaries
cards.prose: As we’ve seen the last few sets, basic landcycling is a very powerful ability, no matter how bad the creature you put it on happens to be. Free Borg Revolutionaries also happens to be quite a powerful creature when you play it. +1/+1 to your whole team is very good in the right spot, and a 4/5 for 5 mana isn’t the worst when you consider that the landcycling is the main reason to play it.

cards.name: Humpback Whales
cards.prose: Humpback Whales is blue’s basic landcycler, which already makes it quite playable. A 5/6 vigilance creature with ward is certainly more than nothing should you end up casting it, but the fact that you can use Humpback Whales to fix your mana at any point you draw it makes this card extremely useful for any deck.

cards.name: Rogue Artificial Intelligence
cards.prose: Just like the other landcyclers, the fact that this is mana fixing is the main reason to play it. When you do play it on 6, Rogue Artificial Intelligence will have a significant impact on the board no matter which mode you choose, while also being an artifact creature for the Borg and a dilemma for blue/black. This might actually be the best entry in the cycle.

cards.name: Captain Michael Burnham
cards.prose: The adoptive sister of Spock, Captain Michael Burnham of the U.S.S. Discovery is a somewhat contentious figure in the Star Trek universe, but a capable Captain nonetheless. As for the card, this is a pretty solid payoff for this red/green landfall deck. The points of damage aren’t all that important, but there appears to be a lot of ways to get multiple land drops in a turn and have Michael pick up +1/+1 counters, too. Given that it starts out as a 3/3 with trample, it looks like Burnham will become a threat very quickly.

cards.name: Horta
cards.prose: Poor old Colossal Dreadmaw , another victim of power creep in the 2020s. Horta is a strong creature if you cast it, but the main reason to put it in your deck is because of its landcycling, just like the other entries in this cycle.

cards.name: Savvy Profiteer
cards.prose: Savvy Profiteer is mostly just a 2-drop mana dork in red , which is solid on its own.
