If you have the time, creating Treasure tokens will allow you to build up your mana over a few turns to cast something really big, or it could just give you some stuff to sacrifice. Still, it’s a mana dork, so you’ll play this in every red deck.

cards.name: Cold-Blooded Crew
cards.prose: Our final landcycler, Cold-Blooded Crew looks a fair bit worse than its counterparts in other colors, but that’s neither here nor there. You’ll definitely play it as a way to fix your mana, and if you end up casting it as a 6-drop that can’t be chump blocked, there are far worse things you could do.

cards.name: Moopsy
cards.prose: I get to say this in every set review, but 1-mana 1/1s with deathtouch are really good. Yet none of them have ever been called Moopsy before, which honestly might be worth an extra point on the grade.

cards.name: Mugato
cards.prose: I’m not normally in the habit of giving praise to what’s basically a big vanilla creature, but reach and vigilance is such a deadly combination that I think Mugato is actually better than it looks. It’s so hot right now!

cards.name: Kira Nerys, Firebrand
cards.prose: Kira Nerys, Firebrand is a very unique and interesting design. While it looks powerful for certain Constructed decks, I can’t think of all that many ways to utilize Kira in Limited, mostly just flash creatures or instant-speed token-makers. As a 4/3 trampler for 3 mana, it’s obviously playable, but that might end up being all Kira can be in most cases.

cards.name: The Traveler
cards.prose: I really hoped for more out of the blue/green signpost uncommon. The Traveler has the potential to have a lot of power, but that 3 toughness means you’ll find it difficult to put that power to use, as it trades off with anything that has 3 power of its own. This card is definitely playable, but I really wanted something more interesting.

cards.name: The Holodeck
cards.prose: The Holodeck was probably one the coolest innovations for The Next Generation as it allowed the writers to tell a greater range of stories in the series. The card is extremely powerful, especially as it always allows you to play any basic land from outside the game , and the permanents you get from your graveyard can keep recurring themselves. The problem is simply being able to take a turn off to play a 7-drop that does nothing the turn you play it. That’s an extremely hefty cost, and one that I’m not sure we’ll even be able to pay.

cards.name: Vulcan
cards.prose: Like in any set, dual lands are important for fixing your mana and enabling splashes. These planets can do a little extra as they’re searchable by some cards in TRK and provide additional names towards strange new worlds abilities. You should typically pick these over mediocre commons for your deck, but not over more premium ones, though this dynamic can also shift if there are splash colors that you’re looking to fix for.

cards.name: Marooned
cards.prose: The latest sets have had very good variations on this effect in blue, but Marooned is missing the clause of removing the abilities of the thing it enchants. As it stands, it’s a fine way to remove a creature, but it’s not without significant downsides that will surely hold it back compared to cards like Infinite Coursework .

cards.name: Gray and Adira, Forever Joined
cards.prose: The trouble with cards like this is that while it’s supposed to be a payoff for a noncreature spells deck, it requires you to have creatures to use it with. Cards like that have historically not been good. Don’t get me wrong, there are some great creatures that you could combine with Gray and Adira, Forever Joined , but you’ll need those to justify this card. At the very least it can copy itself so you’ll always get another 2/3 to attack with.

cards.name: Anthropological Mission
cards.prose: Getting to draw a card whenever you play a noncreature spell could be quite powerful. The first two spells only let you loot , but every spell thereafter nets you a whole new card. Anthropological Mission requires a little bit of time to get going, but if you can give it that time, it should be very effective. Load up on beam me up spells if you’re going to build around it.

cards.name: Commander Raffi Musiker
cards.prose: Most of the time, you’re going to want to investigate with Commander Raffi Musiker . A 3-drop Thraben Inspector is pretty strong, even at the cost of 2 life. Exiling something from a graveyard doesn’t seem like it will be as good, but if you have some gravebreak triggered abilities available, I could also see that working. Overall, Raffi covers a lot of bases and slots perfectly into multiple decks as a result.

cards.name: Ravenous Cosmozoan
cards.prose: While the dream is to cast this for just 1 mana, even at 3 or 4, Ravenous Cosmozoan looks like a great card to cast. Flying appears to be at a premium in this set, so a 3/3 flier will go a long way. It won’t take much to set this up to be playable and a really good spells deck might get to utilize it even more.

cards.name: Oberth-Class Starship
cards.prose: It may take a lot to station this little ship, but the fact that it immediately draws you a card (albeit, a basic Plains ) is the key takeaway here. Oberth-Class Starship is a very playable card in any white deck, and there are also some nice synergies to find with it.

cards.name: Saavik, Stoic Student
cards.prose: One could look at Saavik, Stoic Student and see a white Flametongue Kavu . While that may be the case, Saavik is far more situational and quite inefficient. It’s at least two creature types to put towards its federation ability, but if that’s all you have, 2 damage won’t do very much when you’re late enough in the game to cast a 5-drop. There will be plenty of times when Saavik is a great two-for-one play, but also many more when it’ll be stuck in your hand doing not much of anything.

cards.name: There's Coffee in that Nebula
cards.prose: In only the fifth episode of Voyager , the crew find that their energy levels are critically low, meaning Janeway can’t use the replicators to make a good cup of coffee. They find a nearby nebula that they believe can provide them with a new power source, leading to Janeway’s immortal line: There's Coffee in that Nebula . As much as this is a meme (the episode wasn’t particularly good after all), the card itself looks quite strong, essentially like a white Think Twice with a bit of card selection thrown in.

cards.name: Consider the Prime Directive
cards.prose: Most conditional counterspells get significantly worse in the late game, as the more lands your opponent has, the fewer spells you’ll actually be able to counter. However, Consider the Prime Directive is never dead. Stunning a creature and drawing a  card is also a very good mode to have access to. This also causes you to face a dilemma, so it looks like it’ll be really good in the format.

cards.name: Enterprise NX-01
cards.prose: The Enterprise NX-01 was the ship piloted by the crew from Star Trek: Enterprise . This card certainly has the potential to be powerful, but without knowing how fast the format will be, it’s difficult to evaluate. I certainly think being a spacecraft instead of just a creature holds it back a lot, but it’ll be best suited for some sort of tempo deck that can use it to get rid of a blocker and continue applying pressure to an opponent.

cards.name: Federation Probe
cards.prose: Say it with me: “We don’t underestimate 1-drops!” I’m very happy to play Federation Probe on turn 1 and get a surveil along with my flying 1/1, then later in the game it can buff a creature and potentially get a better attack in. But that’s not what makes this card special. It’s a dilemma, a cheap creature to beam up, and a cheap artifact. This looks really good, and my relatively high grade for a common might not even be high enough.

cards.name: Make It So
cards.prose: This is a draw spell I really like. Picard’s catchphrase, Make It So , lets you draw two cards and create a 1/1 token, which sounds pretty good for just 4 mana. It also has you face a dilemma, which makes it very desirable for any decks that care about that. As long as the format is slow enough to allow you to draw cards in this way, this should be a very good card in any blue deck. Bonus points for being part of an infinite combo with Stella Lee, Wild Card .

cards.name: Suus Mahna Practitioner
cards.prose: “Tapper” creatures tend to appear in white, so this card is throwing me off somewhat. The first two land names are pretty trivial, so Suus Mahna Practitioner should never cost more than 3 mana to activate. I also think the third and fourth should be relatively easy to find, so I’m sure we’ll be Vulcan Nerve Pinching our opponents with relative ease.

cards.name: Test of Priorities
cards.prose: Instant speed flicker spells aren’t printed too often anymore, so it’s nice to see this one here. For the most part, Test of Priorities is a cheap cantrip for both the dilemmas deck and the noncreature spells deck. It might be able to save a creature from removal or reuse its abilities, but you’ll use it most often as a cantrip, and that’s probably good enough to play it.

cards.name: Collective Drone
cards.prose: The problem with a 10/2 creature is that as ridiculous as that stat line might seem at first, it still just trades off with other 2-drops in combat. Collective Drone won’t always be that big, but the simple fact that it never gains any toughness makes it fragile. If you can give it some other abilities through your other Borg drones, then it certainly pays you off for that. But until then, it’s little more than a slightly over-statted vanilla creature .

cards.name: De-evolve
cards.prose: This is certainly an interesting way to word a Pacifism in black. For the most part, this will function the same way, but later in the game you’ll get to exile the creature as soon as the turn starts, which is pretty nice. However, De-evolve comes with no protection against the enchanted creature being beamed up, so you have to be very careful to choose your moment. As such, it’s a good removal spell, but there are much better ones.

cards.name: Fugitive Listener
cards.prose: The typical Ravenous Rats design has been losing a bit of luster lately, so changing it up and putting that same ability on a 3-drop with a bit more power sounds alright to me. Fugitive Listener won’t draw you a card, but having your opponent discard one is nearly always just as good, which makes this a premium black common.

cards.name: Pattern Buffer Preservation
cards.prose: This card reminds me a lot of Final Fantasy ’s Resentful Revelation . While Pattern Buffer Preservation doesn’t give you as much card selection, the vastly cheaper beam me up cost means you’ll get to cast both copies of it a lot more often. It’ll almost always be a two-for-one card advantage spell, and I’m sure there are plenty of decks that will want that.

cards.name: Storied Veteran
cards.prose: This aggressive Klingon card does a few things on its own. Firstly, the fact that it can come back makes it an excellent creature to sacrifice. Bringing it back of course causes it to leave the graveyard, so it’s also good in black/green. Being an aggressive creature might make it reasonably playable in the Borg deck too, even though it isn’t an artifact. Storied Veteran looks like a pretty solid little 1-drop to me.

cards.name: Tenacious Drone
cards.prose: While I’d prefer the stats of this creature to be the other way around (a 1/1 that dies into a 2/1), Tenacious Drone is still a high quality 2-drop that doesn’t mind being sacrificed. It clearly should work in the Borg deck, but it’s probably good enough for the Klingon sacrifice deck, too.

cards.name: Vengeance Mission
cards.prose: Building this up to seven quest counters sounds like quite a lot. It’s worth noting that creatures trading off in combat will of course trigger this twice, so maybe seven counters isn’t too difficult, but I’d still view Vengeance Mission as only hitting your opponent for 1 each time it triggers. That’s probably still good enough to play, but we’ve seen significantly better versions of this same effect in the past, so I think its power level is a bit below where it needs to be.

cards.name: Lwaxana Troi, Charming Guest
cards.prose: Lwaxana Troi has Deanna’s mother who could read people’s minds thanks to her Betazoid heritage. As such, she’d often exclaim that Picard or other men around her are thinking about her in a sexual way to embarrass and flirt with them. As such, is it not a bit on the nose that her card, Lwaxana Troi, Charming Guest , can give a bonus to a creature you have as long as this card is… horizontal? Yeah, okay. I think it’s good, don’t get me wrong, just the design is a bit… funny?

cards.name: Perils of the Past
cards.prose: First thing’s first, using this as a combat trick is a bad idea. It should probably be what you do around 5% of the time. About a quarter of the cards in this set are artifacts, which is just enough to make artifact removal look like something you want to put in your main deck. Between the Borg and the spacecraft, there are a lot of good targets. I’d definitely start out by playing the first copy of Perils of the Past in my main deck, and as the format evolves we can adjust that number accordingly.

cards.name: Genesis Device
cards.prose: As a big fan of Scapeshift in Modern, I’m really liking Genesis Device . The machine capable of turning a lifeless planet into a lush paradise, teeming with life, of course can turn all your lands into new ones. I think the main use of this is simply to ramp you like Final Frontier can. However, in a landfall deck specifically, cracking this to get five or six new landfall triggers sounds promising.

cards.name: Stable Wormhole
cards.prose: Stable Wormhole isn’t a card I’d want to put in an average green deck. On balance, it’s likely just worse than Final Frontier . However, the landfall deck in particular is an aggressive one that really wants to hit more land drops, and this does seem like a good way to enable that turn after turn. That seems like a deck that could utilize this to great effect, but I wouldn’t want it anywhere else.

cards.name: Lore, Positronic Provocateur
cards.prose: Lore was essentially Data’s “evil twin brother” and a recurring villain in The Next Generation . Lore, Positronic Provocateur isn’t quite as exciting as the character might have you believe. Both abilities are solid, but not exciting. Given that Lore makes you face a dilemma, it has a clear home in your blue/black decks, but it’s likely not good enough to see play in many other builds.

cards.name: U.S.S. Cerritos, Following Up
cards.prose: I laughed at S.H.I.E.L.D. Helicarrier and called it unplayable. Players were so desperate for flying creatures in Marvel Super Heroes that it actually performed fine, but I still maintain that it was awful. U.S.S. Cerritos, Following Up looks almost identical to that, but it’s a spacecraft rather than a vehicle , which to me makes all the difference. You get your officers up front when you play it, and it shouldn’t take too long for you to find the 6 counters you need to get it running.

cards.name: Loot, Exuberant Explorer
cards.prose: Loot, Exuberant Explorer isn’t bad by any means, but it does almost nothing in the early game. A 1/4 is an okay blocker, but you’re not guaranteed to have enough lands to make use of extra land drops. Late game however, just activating it each turn provides you with free value, so it definitely gets better as you approach the end of the game and need to find a way to win.

cards.name: Command Decision
cards.prose: This looks eerily similar to Surgical Precision , which we just saw in Reality Fracture . Command Decision is a decent removal spell, but one that’s quite situational and might not find a target. Granted, you can cast it to draw a card when that happens, but I’m not in the habit of casting 2-mana cantrips if I can help it.

cards.name: Gwyndala, the Progeny
cards.prose: Gwyndala, the Progeny is a very simple card in Limited. It’s a 2/2 for 2 that leaves behind a very relevant equipment after it’s removed from the field. That’s definitely good, but not too exciting. There isn’t much equipment in Star Trek for its second ability to be of any use in Limited, so it really stops there. Blue decks should play Gwyndala, but they don’t need to go out of their way to pick it up.

cards.name: Open Communications
cards.prose: I love this little card. We’re not typically in the habit of casting 1-mana cantrips without some good reason to do so, but Open Communications will surely act more like a Think Twice . It’s also a great, cheap way to trigger the many cards that care about noncreature spells.

cards.name: Stray from History
cards.prose: I’m never a big fan of Coercion effects, but Soul Salvage is definitely something I can get behind. Stray from History looks like a very solid common that I’ll probably always want at least one copy of in a black deck.

cards.name: Genesis Effect
cards.prose: In Wrath of Khan , the Genesis Effect is the process by which a dead planetoid can be transformed into a planet full of life, but it also destroys any trace of life in its path. As such, the effect of this card is a wonderful top-down design. Six damage for 5 mana is also efficient enough that most red decks should be happy to play the first copy.

cards.name: Tricorder
cards.prose: Short Sword variants crop up time and time again, and they’re usually only slightly outside the realm of what’s playable. I believe Tricorder gives you enough upside on top of your usual +1/+1 to play this in a few decks, though I’d also cut it from plenty of others.

cards.name: Unexplored Territory
cards.prose: While you get access to some mana on the turn you play it, on balance Unexplored Territory is simply worse than an Evolving Wilds , which we have a precedent for in how poor Shire Terrace was in The Lord of the Rings . That’s not to say it’s bad or unplayable, but it doesn’t feel like the easy slam dunk that it could be. Still, it’s good enough for fixing both your mana and your strange new worlds count, so picking one up probably won’t hurt.

cards.name: Dr. Beverly Crusher
cards.prose: An old friend of Captain Picard’s, Dr. Beverly Crusher was the heart of the Enterprise crew for six of the seven seasons of TNG. She was more than just the ship’s doctor; she was often the moral compass that Picard would turn to in his darkest moments. Here, this doctor is an Ajani's Pridemate that also doubles lifegain triggers, so it picks up two +1/+1 counters every time you gain life. That sounds good, but with no lifegain theme to back it up, Dr. Beverly Crusher doesn’t look that good. There are a lot of random lifegain sources, so it should do some work in the right deck, but Star Trek i

cards.name: Set Phasers to . . .
cards.prose: Looks like we’ll have to Set Phasers to . . . kill most of the time. One mana for 3 damage is a very efficient rate for a removal spell, even if you can only use it in combat. And every now and again, picking stun will let you interact favorably with a bigger creature.

cards.name: Emergency Holographic Crew
cards.prose: Spacecraft don’t seem too likely to end up in the graveyard, since you need to station them before they can trade off in combat. That said, getting a sweet two-for-one with Emergency Holographic Crew is hard to pass up. It seems like most of the time you’d have to surveil with it, but hopefully you can wait long enough until you can get back your Suurok-Class Science Vessel or something similar.

cards.name: Ensign Pavel Chekov
cards.prose: This Ensign Pavel Chekov card has quite a unique design. It might be possible to mill out your opponent if you can combine it with other similar effects, but the most important part of Chekov’s effect is the ability to steal a land from your opponent. You’re very likely to find one out of the cards you exile, letting Chekov act as a defensive cantrip creature that advances your gameplan in the Strange New Worlds deck.

cards.name: Highly Illogical
cards.prose: Four mana Cancel s aren’t where we typically want to be, but you can’t cast Cancel on turn 2 to hit a cheap spell. Highly Illogical actually seems like a pretty logical card to play in a blue deck, especially one based around noncreature spells.

cards.name: Cha'DIch Investigator
cards.prose: Five-drops tend to be very replaceable these days, yet Cha'DIch Investigator looks surprisingly good for a common, kind of like Girder Goons from Streets of New Capenna . A 4/4 plus a 2/1 haste creature is worth paying 5 mana for, and I can see this being good top-end for the mana curve of your Klingon aggro decks.

cards.name: Relentless Drednok
cards.prose: It may not have evasion , but getting to play a Relentless Drednok on turn 1, especially in a Borg deck, is a great way to start off your mana curve. Lifelink is very powerful, even on small creatures, and getting to turn it into a free card later in the game makes it a great card to sacrifice, too. It basically does something in nearly every one of black’s themes and that’s worth the grade on its own.

cards.name: Test of Loyalty
cards.prose: Given the black/green theme, I can definitely see wanting there to be a Raise Dead in this format, and here it is. You’ll use Test of Loyalty most often simply to get a creature back, as guaranteeing yourself a castable spell is pretty much always better than drawing a random card. It’s also a cheap spell for noncreature spell synergies and a dilemma for you to face. This is an excellent card that I think a lot of black decks will be after.

cards.name: Starfleet Security
cards.prose: The death trigger is limited to only your turn, but Starfleet Security looks an awful lot like a creature that draws a card when it dies. I don’t make much of it being a 1/1 with haste, but it’s clearly a useful 1-drop that will shine alongside some ways to sacrifice it.

cards.name: Targ Wrangler
cards.prose: Unlike the Pet Sehlat , Targ Wrangler looks extremely good for an oversized 3-drop with a downside. The thing is, we’ve seen a lot of cards act as sacrifice fodder so far, which means it shouldn’t be too hard to negate this drawback completely. As such, this looks a lot like a big 5/3 that’ll trade off with two creatures in combat. It even works really well with stationing spacecraft and the 8-power theme in red/white.

cards.name: Isolinear Processor
cards.prose: We don’t get a lot of 2-drop mana rocks for a very good reason; they’re usually too strong. Isolinear Processor may only be restricted to playing artifacts, but there are a lot of good ones to ramp into, and this can be a good way to enable some of the more powerful artifacts in Star Trek .

cards.name: Command Subadjunct
cards.prose: Vigilance carries a lot of extra weight in this set as it can allow you to attack with your creatures and then station a spacecraft with them afterwards. Even so, Command Subadjunct feels like it’s only slightly better than a vanilla 2/1 for 1, which is very playable, but nothing exciting.

cards.name: Dr. McCoy, Surly Surgeon
cards.prose: I could easily be wrong here, but this kind of effect doesn’t seem very good in the first place and even less good on a creature with such weak stats. It does make it very difficult for your opponent to get into combat with some of your creatures, but unless yours are already big enough, that doesn’t even amount to much. At 3 mana, Dr. McCoy, Surly Surgeon would be efficient enough to take notice of, but at 4 it just seems over-costed and too weak.

cards.name: Data, New Life
cards.prose: I’ve been very wrong about cards like this in the past, so I’m being extra careful with how I rate Data, New Life . It naturally grows every turn just from you drawing your card for the turn, but you’ll really want to combine it with other sources of card draw to make Data really shine. I think that’ll be fine to do, but starting out as a 0/1 will surely hold it back.

cards.name: Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge
cards.prose: Another popular character from TNG, Lt. Cmdr. Geordi La Forge sadly doesn’t have an inspiring card here. Doubling up your station abilities isn’t all that good. I can’t imagine this will be necessary for any blue decks, so even if you do play it, you won’t miss it when you don’t draw it.

cards.name: Melkotian Adjudicator
cards.prose: Since this triggers off not just instants and sorceries, but also some creatures, I quite like it. It’d be easy to compare it to Cetacean Ops , but the fact that it flies makes a big difference. Flying seems especially rare in Star Trek , since many of the fliers require stationing, which makes Melkotian Adjudicator stand out even more.

cards.name: Starfleet Spanner Jockey
cards.prose: On top of being an excellent early blocker, Starfleet Spanner Jockey is quite good at stationing spacecraft. Not being able to attack most of the time might hinder it somewhat, but a 3/3 for 2 mana in Star Trek still has plenty of uses.

cards.name: Assault Drone
cards.prose: +1/+0 to your team certainly isn’t nothing, and the more aggressive you are, the more you’ll appreciate it. But Assault Drone only looks average to me, as not buffing toughness or making your Borg drones more resilient in any way is a shame.

cards.name: Automated Warfare System
cards.prose: This card comes from a very evocative episode of TNG. The crew finds a planet whose population was completely wiped out by automated weaponized drones from a weapons company who just wanted to sell more weapons. Automated Warfare System can cover a few bases as an artifact creature for the Borg and a sacrifice outlet for the Klingons.

cards.name: Tal Shiar Operative
cards.prose: This creature essentially attacks as a 2/2 with deathtouch , which is going to be pretty hard for a lot of opponents to block profitably. As such, Tal Shiar Operative is a simple enough common that can provide you with a repeatable source of dilemmas. That’s definitely useful to some decks.

cards.name: Cantankerous Captain
cards.prose: Cantankerous Captain brings back the design we saw on Valor Singer from Forgotten Realms and adds a pretty mediocre bonus once you have 8 power among your creatures. You’re going to be able to find much better creatures for your aggro decks, but this will fill the curve in fine.

cards.name: Dahar Master
cards.prose: Finding the sacrifice fodder for Dahar Master is the only thing you need to do here. If you sacrifice a creature with 2 power, a Shock in exchange isn’t actually a good trade for you. It’s not that this card is bad, but you need to make sure that what you give up is worth what you get out of it. If you don’t have much to offer to it, this can probably stay in the sideboard.

cards.name: Reckless Impulse
cards.prose: Unlike most draw spells, Reckless Impulse isn’t great to play early in a game. It is, however, a very nice card to draw later in the game, as you’re far more likely to have enough time and mana to play both cards you hit with it. All I’ll say otherwise is to remember not to play your land for turn before playing this, because if you hit two lands with it, you’ll really want to be able to play both over two turns.

cards.name: Silicate Surveyor
cards.prose: Just about any creature that “draws” a card when it enters is worth playing. Silicate Surveyor really pushes that idea to its limit, since a 4/4 reach creature for 5 mana is very far away from something I’d be happy to play otherwise. It’s a fine card, but when it gets this expensive I wonder if we can do better.

cards.name: Test of Identity
cards.prose: Some decks are going to be perfectly happy casting this as Thrill of Possibility , while Klingon decks are going to want it as a cool combat trick that you can essentially cycle. Test of Identity looks like it hits enough notes that it’ll see play, but it’s not something you should go out of your way to pick up.

cards.name: Dominion Supervisor
cards.prose: It’s quite funny to see a big, scary Dominion agent being barely better than the adorable Pridemalkin . Dominion Supervisor is a nice card to curve into naturally, and it might be quite good in the late game when you have multiple creatures to gain trample , but it’s kind of average overall.

cards.name: First Contact
cards.prose: The black/green archetype in Star Trek is all about cards leaving your graveyard, and we’ve seen several payoffs that reward you for that. Funnily enough, not only does First Contact fill your graveyard for this strategy, but the card you get back also comes from your graveyard, so it’ll trigger all of these effects. I doubt I’d want to play this in any other deck, but it does look very nice in black/green.

cards.name: Saurian Explorer
cards.prose: Landfall decks typically suffer from running out of lands and not being able to trigger their abilities anymore. Not only does Saurian Explorer attack as a 6/5 when you can trigger it, or even an 8/7 or 10/9, but its activated ability gives you a guaranteed way to trigger landfall in the late game, which I’m sure the landfall decks are going to want.

cards.name: Xindi Surveyors
cards.prose: I’d call this virtually unplayable in many sets. But in Star Trek , landfall is surprisingly well supported. A turn-3 Xindi Surveyors might end up a 6/5 on turn 4, so I could definitely see this being playable in that deck. But I wouldn’t want to play it elsewhere.

cards.name: Cybernetic Specialist
cards.prose: Cybernetic Specialist is quite unassuming. It’s a strictly better version of Sanitation Automaton from Murders at Karlov Manor , which was a huge overperformer. It has synergy in white-black and green-black, and might be a perfectly fine curve-filler for just about any deck.

cards.name: Impossible Choice
cards.prose: The season two episode of Voyager , “Tuvix”, posited one of the show’s best and most well-known ethical conundrums. Tuvok and Neelix end up fused together into one person, and the entire episode is spent debating whether it’s ethical to split them back into their original selves. I don’t know the answer, but I do know that you should probably pick “remain fused” whenever you play this card, though neither modes of this Impossible Choice look like great options to me.

cards.name: Dathon, His Heart Open
cards.prose: Darmok is a work of art. The Tamarian language and culture is all based around telling stories. In one of the best scenes of the episode, Darmok signals to Picard that he’d like to hear a story from Earth, so Picard tells him the story of Gilgamesh and Enkidu. Sadly, Dathon is injured and doesn’t survive the night. Dathon, His Heart Open is naturally a card that works with sagas. There are 10 of them in Star Trek , so Dathon can do some things, but I don’t know if this will come together in Limited.

cards.name: The Measure of a Man
cards.prose: This iconic TNG episode is one of my favorites by far, but sadly the card version leaves much to be desired. The Measure of a Man would be great if you had a way to bounce or sacrifice it before the final ability goes off, but I don’t think TRK has much of that. Instead, this is mostly just a very slow flicker that comes with a free Clue token , which is far too situational for most decks.

cards.name: Pet Sehlat
cards.prose: There is really not much difference between Pet Sehlat and a vanilla 3/3 with no downside, the latter of which wouldn’t be playable. Raging Kronch was still pretty good almost a decade ago, and this can turbo-station or hit you 8-power payoffs quickly, so it has merit even when it can’t attack. Plus, it can always block without restriction.

cards.name: Una Chin-Riley, Number One
cards.prose: This kind of effect isn’t bad in theory, but costing 5 mana is just far too much for Una Chin-Riley, Number One to be something I’m ever particularly happy to play. I’d assume that you can cast it and get a trigger from it on the same turn, but that’s by no means guaranteed, and a 4/5 isn’t the most interesting of stat lines if it isn’t getting to trigger.

cards.name: Vexing Drone
cards.prose: Tapping an opponent’s creature is a pretty nice ability to have in an aggressive deck, and Vexing Drone has the magic stats of a 2/2 for 2, meaning we’d probably play it regardless. This is a solid creature for the Borg decks that actually gets better later in the game.

cards.name: Those Old Scientists
cards.prose: Those Old Scientists is a fine draw spell if you have something to get back with the second chapter, but it loses you card advantage if you don’t. I don’t think a lot of decks will be interested in playing this, but it’s certainly not out of the question in a good noncreature spells build.

cards.name: Kai Winn, Faithless Leader
cards.prose: To make the most of Kai Winn, Faithless Leader , you’d want some kind of prior knowledge of your opponent’s hand and/or deck. This card gets a lot better in an open decklists environment, but going in blind? It’ll more often than not be a 3/1 for 2 with very little upside. At the very least you can name a common removal spell in your opponent’s colors, but you’ll get it wrong most of the time.

cards.name: Beckett Mariner, Impetuous Ensign
cards.prose: I’m sure I’m missing something having not watched Lower Decks , but Beckett Mariner, Impetuous Ensign ’s card design leaves a little to be desired. It’s basically just a 2/1 with first strike, which is of course a good creature, but it has a lot of extra text that really doesn’t amount to much. Mariner hits your opponent for an extra 2 damage every three times you tap it. That’s it. It’s good enough to play, but it’s not exciting at all.

cards.name: Erica Ortegas, Plucky Pilot
cards.prose: Landfall decks often have difficulty with running out of lands to keep triggering their effects, so Erica Ortegas, Plucky Pilot sounds like a reasonable effect to have access to, since it makes it so that you can keep playing lands every turn. The problem is, as a 3/3 haste creature for 4 mana, it’s a bit too weak to stand on its own. Overall, Ortegas is a weak synergy piece that won’t even be necessary in every landfall deck.

cards.name: Planetary Patrol
cards.prose: Assuming you hit your land drops, at least for the first few turns of the game, Planetary Patrol will basically be a 3/3 for 2 mana whenever it attacks. That’s pretty good, and the base of a 2/2 for 2 is perfectly fine. I don’t know if I necessarily want it outside of a landfall deck, but it does look solid.

cards.name: Final Frontier
cards.prose: I’m very much not a fan of 3-mana Rampant Growth s, but with the strange new worlds and landfall mechanics, plus the fact that this can fetch a planet dual land , I reckon Final Frontier will be one of the better versions of this effect that we’ve ever seen.

cards.name: Neelix, Moral Support
cards.prose: Neelix might be one of the most disliked characters in all of Star Trek ; he’s just kind of annoying and often used as comic relief despite none of the jokes really landing. There’s nothing wrong with Neelix, Moral Support in theory, but aside from the Food token it gives you, there aren’t very many sources of lifegain to help it trigger repeatedly.

cards.name: Photosynthetic Physician
cards.prose: A 5/5 reach creature for 5 mana is alright, but not exciting. What I actually like about Photosynthetic Physician is its graveyard ability, so I’d rather mill or discard it and then have it leave the graveyard for some value and hopefully trigger one of the green/black payoffs for doing so.

cards.name: Class-F Shuttlecraft
cards.prose: We keep getting sets where the generic 3-drop mana rock is actually playable, and I believe this one is too. Class-F Shuttlecraft can fix your mana in any deck you want, but it also gives you the upside of getting to attack later in the game. It doesn’t do a ton, but it certainly gets the job done.

cards.name: Tea, Earl Grey, Hot
cards.prose: Captain Picard’s go-to drink is well known among Trekkies. Tea, Earl Grey, Hot are words uttered in countless episodes of TNG. The card is really good too, you’re probably always happy with a 2-mana artifact that draws a card in any deck that cares about noncreature spells or artifacts.

cards.name: Warp Core
cards.prose: Using Warp Core to find a basic land makes it playable in a lot of different decks. I’m intrigued by its ability to station your spacecraft though, as doing so with any excess mana you have will take a lot of pressure away from your creatures. This is an interesting card for sure, and one that might play a pivotal role within the set.

cards.name: Temporal Anomaly
cards.prose: These utility lands are pretty interesting as far as cycles go. They’re remarkably similar to the “blighted” lands from Battle for Zendikar , but sacrificing them doesn’t put you down on lands. Colorless lands do come with a hefty cost because they don’t fix your colors, but I think you should be able to afford the occasional copy in a 2-color deck, given that their abilities are all quite strong.

cards.name: Hull Breach
cards.prose: I think it’s worth main-decking artifact removal in Star Trek , and Hull Breach is certainly good enough for that. If you manage to catch a strong enchantment at the same time, then all the better.

cards.name: Culber and Stamets, Star-Crossed
cards.prose: As I watched Discovery , I felt entranced by the beautiful love story between Hugh Culber and Paul Stamets. They go through so many hardships and yet always manage to find each other again, and it was wonderful to watch. Sadly, Culber and Stamets, Star-Crossed doesn’t look like a very good card. A 3/4 plus a +1/+1 counter is fine for 4 mana, but the additional mana mode is baffling to say the least. I think you’ll generally be able to do better than this one.

cards.name: Dominion Assault Force
cards.prose: A 4/4 vigilance creature for 4 isn’t exactly terrible, though I do wish it did a little more than that. A free surveil is definitely nice to have, but not something that elevates Dominion Assault Force beyond being a simple vanilla creature.

cards.name: Support Mission
cards.prose: I hate playing cards like this. Support Mission does nothing to affect the board on the turn you play it, and that’s the key problem here. While all the mission cards in this cycle have that drawback, they all make up for it by having considerably better effects than this does. This simply feels like something you should leave in the sideboard and move on.

cards.name: DOT-7 Repair Squad
cards.prose: Untapping a creature for 2 mana and only at sorcery speed sounds kind of useless to me, but it can be helpful if you want to station a spacecraft. Aside from that, DOT-7 Repair Squad doesn’t look very good at all and will probably be quite bad. That said, I thought the same about Wakandan Drone Flock , and that ended up being very good within the context of Marvel Super Heroes , so you never know.

cards.name: Emergency Medical Hologram
cards.prose: Emergency Medical Hologram is such an unassuming 1-drop that I think it might actually be good enough. Putting its +1/+1 counter on itself isn’t the best play you could make, as a 1/2 on the board is very weak. However, putting it on just about any other creature later in the game is bound to be annoying, especially if it helps a creature attack into opposing blockers. It’s also an artifact creature for the Borg decks, which is bound to be relevant.

cards.name: Cloistered Telepath
cards.prose: I’m not quite sure where Cloistered Telepath will fit in this format, but decent triggered ability like this makes it a good option for beam me up spells. It’s quite weak though, so I think I’ll cut this more often than not.

cards.name: Battle-Scarred Survivalist
cards.prose: I get that the Klingon deck is going to have a sacrifice theme, but I don’t think Battle-Scarred Survivalist looks that good. We’ve seen Unruly Mob in past sets be virtually unplayable, and this feels like a watered down version of that. Having menace and the right support at least bumps it up a grade, but I’d need to see this Klingon deck in action before I rate it any higher.

cards.name: Obsidian Order Operative
cards.prose: Facing dilemmas in TRK seems fairly trivial to do. I like having access to a trigger that drains my opponent with each dilemma I face, and a 2/5 makes for a fairly resilient blocker, but Obsidian Order Operative isn’t exciting me like it should. It’s a bit dull, and very cuttable, but it does at least do something that I might want in my dilemma decks.

cards.name: Captain's Tutelage
cards.prose: We’ve seen plenty of cards similar to Captain's Tutelage in the past, and they’ve never really panned out. An effect like this isn’t exactly guaranteed to win a combat for you, and you certainly won’t win the next after it has resolved. Whether or not I bump this grade up or even further down depends completely on how well-placed combat tricks end up being in the format.

cards.name: Quark, Humble Proprietor
cards.prose: I really don’t know what to make of Deep Space Nine ’s humble Ferengi barkeep, Quark, Humble Proprietor . It’s a really unique design that basically requires you to sacrifice it at some point to accomplish anything at all. But even when you do, your only reward is a bunch of Treasure tokens. I can see Quark being a great card in a dedicated sacrifice deck, where the Treasures act as perfect sacrifice fodder, but in your average red deck, I think it falls well short of the mark.

cards.name: Astute Terraformer
cards.prose: Rootwalla and similar creatures get to use threat of activation to attack past bigger creatures in the early turns of a game. Astute Terraformer doesn’t, as its ability is still too expensive to activate that early in most games. This isn’t the kind of benefit you need or even want in a Strange New Worlds deck, though 2/2 with upside is still a solid baseline.

cards.name: Type-2 Phaser
cards.prose: I’m not sure we’ll be setting our phasers to stun any time soon. While it’s cool that this stuns a creature when it enters, I can’t help but be put off by that expensive equip cost. Type-2 Phaser does some good things, but 3 to equip when it doesn’t give any boosts to toughness feels a bit too much.

cards.name: Rules of Acquisition
cards.prose: For the most part, Rules of Acquisition looks unplayable to me. Stealing an opponent’s creature is an extremely powerful effect, but allowing your opponent to draw three cards in exchange feels like a trade I never want to make. I think the best way to use this would be to donate something to your opponent and draw three cards, but that’s still not a good exchange unless you give away something truly useless. Overall, it’s just not worth it without some specific use.

cards.name: Federation Resupply
cards.prose: A one-off conditional tutor spell isn’t worth spending your mana on, even if what you search for is really powerful. However, Federation Resupply lets you search for two things overall, kind of like a white Mystical Teachings . Is that good enough? I could definitely see running it in a deck that had several things to search for, but most of time this is going to be far too weak.

cards.name: Pure Energy
cards.prose: I was a fan of Predictive Preparations in Reality Fracture , though it didn’t really perform well, but I’m not a fan of Pure Energy . The fact that you need three creatures in play to beam it up (one to beam up and the other two to target) really doesn’t inspire me with any hope. I’d leave this one in the sideboard for now.

cards.name: The Naked Time
cards.prose: The Naked Time was the fourth episode of the original series of Star Trek . In this episode, an infection spreads throughout the crew leaving them feeling intoxicated, leading to all sorts of weird incidents. This card, unfortunately, doesn’t look very good. It does a few things, but none of them are worth spending a whole card to get them. Maybe a dedicated landfall deck can make sure of the extra mountain on chapter one.

cards.name: Sisay, Weatherlight Captain
cards.prose: If you’re able to activate the ability of Sisay, Weatherlight Captain , it can definitely be very powerful. But all five colors is a big ask, so I don’t think it’s very likely to happen. The Strange New Worlds archetype might be able to make this work, but it’s a long shot at best. The sheer number of legends, especially hybrid ones, might actually get Sisay up to a 4/4 or 5/5.

cards.name: Drivnod, Carnage Dominus
cards.prose: There are a few death triggers in this set, but Drivnod, Carnage Dominus doing barely anything else isn’t a great look. At 3 toughness, it really needs that indestructible counter to survive and even then, there are still plenty of ways to answer it. I could see it doing some work in the right deck, but a lot has to go right before I’d feel happy about it.

cards.name: Shuttle Ace
cards.prose: I don’t see Shuttle Ace being very playable. It’s a very replaceable 5-drop, and it gives very little value when you play it. It’s just very unexciting, and I think we can move on.

cards.name: Tactical Officer
cards.prose: As a 2-mana 2/1, Tactical Officer really needs to make use of its ability. Unfortunately, that ability isn’t even active until you have a board full of creatures, so I don’t think this is something you want to play unless you just really need a 2-drop .

cards.name: Test of Conviction
cards.prose: Symmetrical draw spells , even ones that aren’t entirely symmetrical, are never very good. As such, we’re really looking at Test of Conviction as a spell that distributes +1/+1 counters, which frankly isn’t very good either. I think this one is going to fall short of the mark, but if the counters deck really needs an effect like this, at least it’s here.

cards.name: Cetacean Ops
cards.prose: We’ve seen a few 3-mana 2/2s in recent sets that pick up a +1/+1 counter whenever you cast a noncreature spell, and they’ve all been bad. Cetacean Ops being a 4-mana 3/3 actually makes me less inclined to want to play it. If I had H.M.S. Bounty, Unlikely Timeship available, then I might be a little more interested, but it’s still not a very good card.

cards.name: Deep Space Scan
cards.prose: If this format is as slow as I suspect it will be, Deep Space Scan could actually be very powerful. However, requiring at least four or five different lands and a slow enough format to accommodate it doesn’t sound like a winning combination to me. I’m sure this could be good in the right deck, but as I’ve said, I don’t think that’ll come up all too often.

cards.name: Red Alert!
cards.prose: Okay, Red Dwarf is the first thing I think of when I hear “Red Alert!”, not Star Trek , but so be it. This card is crap anyway. Trumpet Blast is basically never playable and getting a cost reduction on the worst turn to play it isn’t even an upside.

cards.name: I'm a Doctor, Not a . . .
cards.prose: It’s great to see another of McCoy’s favorite phrases immortalized on a card like this, but sadly, the card just isn’t very good. It may leave a +1/+1 counter behind, but I'm a Doctor, Not a . . . is still a very mediocre combat trick that I’m not going to want to play very often.

cards.name: Warp Speed
cards.prose: At first glance, Warp Speed seems like it’s doing a lot. It fetches you a land , it guarantees your lands all enter play untapped, and it can turn itself into two extra cards in the late game. The problem is that it costs 3 mana to not affect the board and to not accelerate your mana, and that is not good. I could be wrong about this, but I think there are far better ways to enable strange new worlds in this set and this, sadly, won’t be good enough.

cards.name: Live Long and Prosper
cards.prose: You can clearly see what they were trying to do with this card. Doubling your life total means to live long and doubling the cards in your hand means to prosper. I get it, but what if your life total is low and you have no cards in hand? It’s almost like saying you can only Live Long and Prosper if you’re already prosperous and healthy, and that’s not something I can get on board with.

cards.name: A Good Day to Die
cards.prose: Even just for 1 mana, A Good Day to Die isn’t a combat trick I’m ever happy to play. We’ve seen some defensible versions of this effect in the past, but they all do much better than simply drawing you a card, like leaving a token behind or reanimating the creature. This new version just doesn’t cut it for me.

cards.name: Dathon and Picard at El-Adrel
cards.prose: TNG’s season five episode “Darmok” is probably my favorite in the entire franchise. In it, the Enterprise encounters the Tamarians, a race whose language is seemingly impossible for them to decipher. It turns out that the Tamarians are storytellers and they speak entirely in metaphors and story references, kind of like how many people today communicate through memes. “Temba, His Arms Wide” means to give something and “Shaka, When the Walls Fell” means to fail. It’s a wonderful episode that really highlights Patrick Stewart’s raw acting talent. Anyway, Dathon and Picard at El-Adrel is a pretty

cards.name: Peace in Our Time
cards.prose: This is a cool build-around that might be worth building around, but the idea of letting my opponent draw cards for free doesn’t really inspire me with confidence. Peace in Our Time just seems far too cute, especially against an opponent that could potentially find a removal spell for it before it gets up to 12 counters. I’ll be trying this alternate wincon for myself, but I recommend others stay away from it.

cards.name: Dominion Infiltration
cards.prose: Creating temporary clones like this isn’t a winning play, especially when you need to target your opponent’s creatures with it. You have no control over how good Dominion Infiltration will be when you maindeck it, which is a surefire recipe for a terrible, unplayable card.

cards.name: Combadge
cards.prose: I get the gimmick, I really do, but Combadge feels embarrassingly bad. You have to pay 3 mana to cast it, and then spend 4 mana equipping both copies to your creatures to make them both unblockable . Except that disrupting one of them disrupts the other. Your opponent could even remove one of the communicators, and then the other one does absolutely nothing. This feels like a big miss to me.

cards.name: Kobayashi Maru Scenario
cards.prose: The Kobayashi Maru Scenario is a test given to Starfleet cadets that have command ambitions. It’s an unwinnable test designed to have the cadet experience fear in the face of certain death. If you hope not to lose to it, you’ll have to find a way to beat it. There are some ways, like Rules of Acquisition and Kirk, Commanding Officer , but without them, playing this card will cause you to lose far too often.

cards.name: Vulcan Mind-Meld
cards.prose: The Vulcan Mind-Meld is a skill whereby Vulcans can share their thoughts with other living beings and vice versa. This card is a very cool top-down design of that idea, but essentially letting my opponent draw a card feels like too high a price for me to draw two, especially when they don’t even come from my own library.

cards.name: Test of Courage
cards.prose: While I think artifact removal is worth main-decking in TRK, one as restrictive as this doesn’t seem good enough. Test of Courage feels like a solid sideboard card and nothing more.

cards.name: Sen Triplets
cards.prose: Sen Triplets is, as I understand it, a much-maligned commander. Getting to play cards from an opponent’s hand in a 4-player game can be pretty nasty. In 1v1 Limited, it’s just not as good. I can definitely see the potential, but a 3-color card that does nothing until the turn after you’ve played it doesn’t sound very good to me.

cards.name: Isshin, Two Heavens as One
cards.prose: Isshin, Two Heavens as One is a difficult card to get right. In the context of this set, you’re mostly looking at the attack triggers from cards in the red/white archetype, but splashing black in an aggressive Boros deck might not be possible. I’d love to see it happen, but I don’t think it will.

cards.name: The Needs of the Many
cards.prose: In the climax of The Wrath of Khan , Spock sacrifices his own life to save the Enterprise crew from Khan’s final gambit. With his final, dying breath, he simply reminds Kirk that “ The Needs of the Many outweigh the needs of the few, or the one.” This card isn’t particularly good. Protecting your whole team isn’t a particularly desirable effect in Limited. Board wipes are pretty rare, and sacrificing a creature to use this effect isn’t good enough either. The card is incredibly thematic, but simply not good.

cards.name: Troubling Tribbles
cards.prose: The tribbles are a weird creature in Star Trek lore that multiply exceedingly quickly. Troubling Tribbles does exactly that, but they’re next to useless when they do. After a few turns, if they aren’t dealt with, you might have four, eight, or even 16 of them, but they have 0 power and can’t block, so what good are they? If you can find a way to mass pump them, this card might actually be useful, but that’s not trivial to do. That said, I can’t wait to beat an opponent with an army of tribbles!

cards.name: Branching Timeline
cards.prose: Eight-mana spells need to have some guarantee of winning the game for you to want to bother accelerating into them. Branching Timeline does nothing of the sort and is entirely random, which makes it completely unplayable.

cards.name: Brazen Bluff
cards.prose: I absolutely love the design of this card. Big bluffs like this were a quintessential part of Captain Kirk’s character and style of command. Sadly, the most common outcome of Brazen Bluff is basically a Negate , so it’s not at all playable in Limited. I’m looking forward to playing it in Standard , though.

cards.name: Infinite Diversity
cards.prose: As noble a cause as Infinite Diversity is, it’s a 9-mana spell. It’s pretty close to uncastable in most situations, and it requires a good spell to copy and plenty of creatures in play to fuel it, all of which add up to an unplayable mythic .

cards.name: Year of Hell
cards.prose: Certainly my favorite episode of Voyager , this two-parter sees Janeway and the crew navigating through the space of a hostile race with temporal manipulating weapons for an entire year. These people have used their weapons to erase entire enemy races from history, and now they’re trying to do the same to Voyager . Over the Year of Hell , Voyager loses countless fights and falls further and further into disrepair as you see the strain this puts on the whole crew. It’s an epic spectacle, but apparently not epic enough to make a remotely playable saga out of it.

cards.name: Starfleet Academy
cards.prose: For Starfleet Academy to net you any mana, you need to have at least seven different creature types in play. While that’s not impossible, it doesn’t sound very likely at all, and even when that happens you’d need mana sinks to make it matter. This looks completely unplayable to me, and harder to enable than similar lands of the past that were also useless in Limited.

cards.name: Flare of Fortitude
cards.prose: While casting this for no mana is quite interesting, the effect isn’t. Flare of Fortitude isn’t something you should put in your deck, no matter how you end up casting it.

cards.name: Arcum Dagsson
cards.prose: Since there are some expensive noncreature artifacts in TRK that we’d really like to cheat out , such as The Holodeck and Deep Space 9 , I could see Arcum Dagsson playing a role every now and again. However, in a vast majority of cases, turning your creatures into noncreatures isn’t something you can afford to do in Limited. This is a big miss.

cards.name: Bruvac the Grandiloquent
cards.prose: I absolutely love Bruvac the Grandiloquent . It’s in fact my main commander. But there are literally zero cards in this set that combine with it. Unless you really want to play Zachary Quinto as a Horned Turtle , you should never play this.

cards.name: Captain Sisay
cards.prose: Captain Sisay looks like it should be good in a set with so many legendary cards in it, but this card is just outdated and weak. Four mana for a 2/2 is very bad, and it doesn’t do anything until you get to untap with it. It’s a hard pass from me.
